  3. Marcado de artefactos como "pinned": el proceso PowerShell final bloquea versiones críticas en el repositorio interno, impidiendo su eliminación o sobreescritura accidental. Este control asegura la trazabilidad y disponibilidad de versiones certificadas.

docs.title: 4. Auditorías y trazabilidad
docs.text:
Cada etapa del SDLC está registrada en el sistema de integración continua, lo que permite auditar:

  • Tiempos de ejecución
  • Resultados de pruebas
  • Logs de compilación y publicación
  • Versiones generadas
  • Cambios en configuraciones

El pipeline impide el avance a la siguiente fase si un paso no se ejecuta correctamente, lo que constituye un control de flujo de seguridad y evidencia de cumplimiento de buenas prácticas DevSecOps.

docs.title: 5. Conclusiones
docs.text:
El modelo de desarrollo seguro de Flexygo incorpora mecanismos de seguridad, control y trazabilidad en todo el ciclo de vida del software. Las evidencias muestran la aplicación sistemática de medidas de protección de la información, control de versiones, auditoría de código y validación de artefactos.

Este proceso cumple con los principios de un SDLC seguro, alineado con estándares internacionales como OWASP SAMM, ISO/IEC 27034 y NIST SP 800-218 (SSDF), aportando garantías de integridad, trazabilidad y seguridad del software producido.

docs.title: Gestión de vulnerabilidades
docs.text: En Flexygo, la gestión de vulnerabilidades es un proceso clave dentro del ciclo de vida del desarrollo seguro (SecDevOps). Este proceso asegura la detección temprana, evaluación, priorización y remediación de las vulnerabilidades presentes en el código o en los entornos de despliegue, garantizando así la integridad, disponibilidad y confidencialidad de las aplicaciones.

docs.title: 1. Detección de vulnerabilidades con SonarQube
docs.text:
Flexygo utiliza SonarQube como herramienta principal para el análisis estático de código. Este sistema se integra directamente en los pipelines de desarrollo y cumple con las siguientes funciones:

  • Análisis automático del código fuente en cada commit o pull request, detectando vulnerabilidades, code smells y malas prácticas de seguridad.
  • Evaluación de calidad basada en reglas de seguridad OWASP y estándares internacionales (CWE, SANS).
  • Generación de informes de riesgo, los cuales son revisados por el equipo de desarrollo y seguridad antes de aprobar la integración al entorno principal.
  • Alertas y métricas: SonarQube notifica automáticamente a los responsables cuando se detectan vulnerabilidades críticas o bloqueantes.

docs.title: 2. Integración con el ciclo SecDevOps
docs.text:
La estrategia de SecDevOps implementada en Flexygo permite que la seguridad esté presente desde las primeras etapas del desarrollo. Los principios clave incluyen:

  • Shift-Left Security: la detección y remediación se realiza en fases tempranas del desarrollo, reduciendo costos y tiempos.
  • Automatización de pruebas: los pipelines de CI/CD ejecutan de manera automática análisis de seguridad y validaciones previas al despliegue, lanzando scripts de ataque sobre cada versión final.
  • Colaboración multidisciplinar: los equipos de desarrollo, operaciones y seguridad trabajan de manera conjunta para asegurar que las vulnerabilidades se gestionen de forma eficiente y transparente.

docs.title: 3. Remediación y despliegue con GitFlow y Hotfix
docs.text:
En caso de detectar una vulnerabilidad crítica en el exterior, se sigue un flujo estructurado de remediación basado en GitFlow:

  1. Creación de rama Hotfix: se genera una rama específica a partir de main o release para abordar el problema sin interferir con el desarrollo en curso.
  2. Corrección y validación: el equipo de desarrollo implementa la solución y ejecuta nuevamente los análisis de SonarQube para verificar la efectividad del parche.
  3. Despliegue inmediato (Hotfix): una vez validada la corrección, se realiza un despliegue inmediato al entorno de producción mediante el pipeline automatizado.
  4. Merge controlado: la rama Hotfix se integra posteriormente en develop y main, garantizando que el código corregido esté sincronizado en todas las ramas activas.

docs.title: 4. Mitigación y medidas preventivas
docs.text:
Además de los procesos de detección y remediación, Flexygo implementa mecanismos activos de mitigación que permiten proteger el entorno en tiempo real frente a intentos de explotación. El sistema monitoriza cada request entrante, analizando sus parámetros y comportamientos. Si se identifica un patrón sospechoso o indicios de ataque —como inyección de código, manipulación de cabeceras o intentos de acceso no autorizados— la petición es bloqueada de inmediato. Asimismo, si se detectan cinco peticiones sospechosas provenientes de una misma IP en un minuto, el sistema procede a bloquear automáticamente dicha dirección IP como medida preventiva.

Adicionalmente, para evitar ataques de fuerza bruta, Flexygo aplica un bloqueo temporal de usuario tras cinco intentos fallidos de autenticación, impidiendo accesos reiterados y reduciendo significativamente el riesgo de compromiso de credenciales. Estas medidas, combinadas con la detección temprana y la respuesta automatizada, fortalecen la postura de seguridad global del ecosistema Flexygo.

docs.title: Requisitos para la certificación de un nuevo producto Flexygo
Requisitos para la certificación de un nuevo producto Flexygo
Descripción general
docs.text:
Para certificar un producto en fábrica y publicarlo en el marketplace, se deben cumplir varios requisitos y presentar demostraciones comerciales y técnicas (pueden ser online).

Todos los productos certificados deben partir de Flexygo como NuGet; el desarrollo partiendo como base de otro producto Flexygo no se certificará.

docs.title: Marketing
docs.text:
• Nombre del producto
  • Estructura de tarifas
  • Logo
  • Texto promocional
  • Vídeo promocional

docs.title: Requisitos técnicos
docs.text:
• Instalable* (depende de fábrica)
  • Publicar un NuGet en repositorio público
  • Despliegue continuo (actualizaciones automáticas)
  • Seguridad implementada (roles/perfiles)
  • Demostración funcional de la aplicación
  • Testing con mínimos demostrables
  • Incorporar cadena de licenciamiento* (depende de fábrica)

docs.title: Recomendaciones
docs.text:
• Interfaz amigable (UI/UX)
  • Despliegue continuo de base de datos
  • Documentación funcional y técnica
  • Vídeos funcionales
  • Roadmap del producto

* Los puntos marcados con asterisco son responsabilidad de fábrica y se proporcionan tras completar la certificación.

docs.title: Procedimiento completo
docs.text:
Antes de empezar a realizar el hotfix, hacemos un pull de develop y master y nos aseguramos de estar al día:

Hacemos clic en GitFlow > Start new hotfix

Definimos el nombre empezando por HOTFIX_ (en mayúsculas) seguido de una breve descripción que sirva como identificador de la rama. Pulsamos OK.

Publicamos las bases de datos del proyecto, establecemos el origin correcto, realizamos el arreglo y descargamos los cambios, tal y como lo haríamos en una nueva funcionalidad.

Revisamos los cambios pendientes y marcamos aquellos que correspondan con el arreglo.

Realizamos un commit empezando el mensaje por la etiqueta FIX: seguido de la descripción del arreglo (el síntoma que veía el usuario). Las notas de la versión solo recogen los commits FT:, FIX:, HL: y DEP:; ver ¿Cómo desarrollar en GIT?.

Hacemos un fetch y revisamos que no tengamos ningún pull pendiente; en caso contrario, nos situamos en la rama correspondiente, realizamos un pull y volvemos a la rama del hotfix.

Pulsamos en Git Flow > Finish Hotfix

Realizamos push en develop, nos situamos en master y realizamos push de master.

docs.title: 1. Crear la release en SourceTree
docs.text:
Se debe partir de la rama develop, limpia y sin cambios pendientes.

  • Pulsar el botón Git-Flow

  • Confirmar la pantalla emergente con OK

  • Volver a pulsar Git-Flow

  • Seleccionar Start New Release e introducir un nombre como RELEASE_4_11_0_1

Se crea una nueva rama a partir de develop. En ella se realizan las pruebas y correcciones necesarias mediante commits normales hasta validar la release.

  • Volver a pulsar Git-Flow y seleccionar Finish Release

  • Confirmar el merge hacia master y develop con el etiquetado correspondiente

Antes de hacer push

Antes de realizar el push, se debe completar el paso siguiente sobre TeamCity.

docs.title: 2. Actualizar el número de versión en TeamCity
docs.text:
• Ir al proyecto de la rama develop → Edit settings
  • Cambiar los dos primeros números del Build Number format (por ejemplo, de 4.10 a 4.11) y resetear el Build Counter a 1
  • Repetir el mismo proceso en el proyecto de la rama master → Edit settings
  • Cambiar el formato (por ejemplo, de 4.10.0 a 4.11.0) y resetear el contador

docs.title: 3. Volver a SourceTree
docs.text:
• Realizar el push de los merges pendientes
  • Verificar que TeamCity compila y publica correctamente

docs.title: Prefijos de commit para las notas de la release
docs.text:
El asunto de cada commit empieza por un prefijo. Con él, el texto del commit se incluye automáticamente en las notas de la versión (de la aplicación, de la ayuda y del paquete NuGet):

  • FT: designa una funcionalidad nueva o una mejora que el usuario puede ver
  • FIX: indica la corrección de un problema identificado; se describe el síntoma que veía el usuario
  • HL: marca uno de los destacados de la versión (unos pocos por versión). Además de la nota, abre el resumen y la noticia de la versión y genera una página de la ayuda
  • DEP: marca características que quedan obsoletas o fuera de catálogo, y qué usar en su lugar
  • INT: trabajo interno (refactorizaciones, compilación, tests, herramientas, documentación interna). Nunca aparece en las notas de la versión

Las notas se escriben solo a partir del asunto y del cuerpo del commit, nunca del código: hay que contar qué cambia para el usuario, no qué clases se han tocado.

docs.title: Reglas que comprueba el repositorio
docs.text:
El hook commit-msg del repositorio de Flexygo (.githooks/commit-msg) rechaza el commit si no las cumple:

  • El asunto empieza por uno de los prefijos anteriores (salvo los merges y los reverts).
  • El asunto tiene más de 50 caracteres (conviene no pasar de unos 72).
  • Ninguna línea contiene ... como relleno.
  • Un commit HL: añade al menos una imagen (.png, .jpg, .jpeg o .gif) en release-notes/images/.

docs.title: Commits HL:
docs.text:
El cuerpo de un HL: sigue una estructura fija, porque con él (y con su captura) se escriben la nota destacada, la noticia y la página de la ayuda:

Text Only
HL: Update Flexygo from a guided wizard with automatic rollback

What: A wizard updates the frontend, the backend and the database in one go, checks the
requirements and the locks first, and rolls the update back when it does not finish.
Where: Admin > Maintenance > Versions, button "Update".
How:
1. Open the Versions page and choose the version to install.
2. Review the requirements and the locks the wizard detects.
3. Start the update and follow its progress; the log can be filtered.
Settings: Repository and credentials of the packages in the updater settings.
Permissions: Administrators only.
Help: Maintenance and updates
  • What, Where y How son obligatorios; Settings, Permissions y Help, solo cuando aplican.
  • La captura es obligatoria y va en el mismo commit, en release-notes/images/, con un nombre descriptivo en minúsculas y con guiones (update-wizard.png).

docs.title: Introduction to Flexygo
docs.text:
Download the installer

You can download the official Flexygo installer to quickly get started with your development environment. 👉 Download installer

See the full Installer guide to learn about all its options (IIS, Docker, migration, uninstall).

Flexygo is an AI Low-Code platform to build products fast thanks to it's easy to use interface, you can build anything with little to no knowdlege about HTML, CSS, JS or C#. But if you ever want to develop more complex applications you'll have access to all of them so you can create the exact idea you had in mind.

  • Modules

    Get to know every flexygo module

  • Form Controls

    Discover every flexygo custom controls

  • Good practices

    Remind yourself of good practices when developing with flexygo

  • Offline App

    Learn to build an app to work with your Flexygo data even in low connectivity locations

docs.title: 🔄 Architecture evolution
docs.text:
Flexygo has evolved from the classic .NET Framework-based model into a completely new architecture based on .NET 9.

Until now, the Flexygo model consisted of a single web application that contained the frontend, the backend and all its libraries within the same site.

With the new architecture, Flexygo is split into:

  • 🖥️ Frontend: the web interface the user sees
  • ⚙️ Backend: the server-side logic and APIs
  • 🛢️ Database

This modular approach serves several key goals:

  • Security: by separating the components, you can host the frontend on a different server than the backend and the database. If the frontend server were compromised, there would be no direct access to the data or the internal logic.
  • Scalability: you can distribute the parts of the system across different physical or virtual environments.
  • Flexibility: it allows deploying customized solutions adapted to each customer or environment.
  • Performance and maintenance: using .NET 9 lets us work with the latest improvements in the .NET ecosystem in terms of performance, cross-platform support and ease of deployment.

Building on this foundation, Flexygo keeps modernizing its whole ecosystem, securing its future and adapting it to today's enterprise development standards.

docs.title: 🚀 How is Flexygo deployed?
docs.text:
You have several options to run or deploy your Flexygo solution:

  • Installer — Ideal for Windows environments. Includes basic IIS, advanced IIS and Docker-via-installer modes. Automates the whole configuration.
  • Docker — Perfect for cloud deployment, Linux environments or container-based automated solutions.
  • Kestrel — Runs directly with dotnet run, ideal for development environments or reverse-proxy solutions.

See the Deployment section of the menu for detailed guides on each option.

docs.title: Flexygo's technologies
docs.text: Flexygo is engineered on the .NET core framework, providing a modern, cross-platform, and high-performance foundation. Its native compatibility with both SQL Server and Oracle databases offers significant architectural flexibility.

docs.title: Front End
docs.text: When developing a Flexygo product front-end you'll be able to use Flexygo's own tools like prebuilt modules and components. Also you'll have acces to HTML, CSS, JS and Bootstrap.

docs.title: Back End
docs.text: As Flexygo has been developed in .NET Core it does admit creating DLL process in C# or vb.net, and also admits stored procedures from SQL Server and Oracle as previously mentioned.

docs.title: Objects
docs.text:
FlexyGo Objects are the fundamental building blocks for creating applications in FlexyGo. Each object corresponds to a main element of your business—like a Customer, Project, or Invoice—and bundles everything needed to manage it: its data structure, input forms, list views, reports, and related processes.

By configuring these reusable objects, you can rapidly build tailored web applications without extensive coding, ensuring consistency and saving development time.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text: Flexygo products are built using modules which are easy to configure components with lots of differents capabilities like showing charts, creaing a Kanban, showing maps with locations and routes and lots more.

docs.title: Creating Reports
docs.text: Flexygo does also have the possibilty of creatintg your own reports in HTML, Power BI, DevExpress and Crystal Reports.

docs.title: Offline Application
docs.text: Flexygo does also have the possibilty of creating an aside mobile app to be accessed offline allowing to continue working even in remote places with low connectivity.

docs.title: Technologies
docs.text: Flexygo's Offline app does use Ionic at is base, with Capacitor and Stencil. It also uses SQLite as its way to store the data that will come in a synchronization with your Flexygo project.

docs.title: Development
docs.text: Flexygo's Offline app product development requires of a bigger programming knowdledge as the pages must be built with HTML, CSS, JS and Ionic knowdlege.

docs.title: Tracking
docs.text: Flexygo's Offline app has tracking functionality which allows getting the exact location data of the configured devices even when the app is closed. It can be configured to just track during ceratin periods of time.

docs.title: More information
docs.text: Besides the technical documentation gathered under Help, this site includes dedicated documentation on Deployment, Product Development, CI/CD and Troubleshooting, as well as the More information section, with additional content about Flexygo: frequently asked questions, trivia ("Did you know...?"), release notes, security guides and the CI/CD cycle, among others.

docs.title: Flexygo architecture 10.0+
docs.text:
Since version 10, Flexygo runs on .NET 9, the current Microsoft platform, instead of .NET Framework. It is faster and safer, and it keeps receiving updates from Microsoft.

The application is split into three parts that can run together on one server or each on its own:

Part What it does Frontend What the browser opens: the screens, the menus and the skin, and the setup and version wizards. It does not connect to the database: it asks the backend for everything. Backend Does the work: the logic, the security, the processes, the scheduled jobs and the reports. It also serves the WebAPI and the MCP server for integrations. SQL Server Keeps the configuration of the application and the data of the product.

Keeping them apart lets you, for example, place the frontend on a server reachable from outside and the backend and the database on the internal network, or give more resources only to the part that does most of the work.

docs.title: Where it can be installed
docs.text:
• IIS, on Windows: the installer does everything. In basic IIS mode the frontend and the backend share one site; in advanced IIS they can go on different sites or servers.
  • Docker: the frontend and the backend in containers, with the database outside Docker in production. See Deployment with Docker.
  • Standalone service (Kestrel), on Windows or Linux, usually behind a reverse proxy such as nginx. It has no installer of its own. See Deployment with Kestrel and Reverse proxy.

Before installing, check the system requirements.

docs.title: Updating
docs.text: Flexygo is updated from the application itself with the version wizard, which checks the requirements before it starts and can undo an update. See Flexygo Updater.

docs.title: System Requirements
docs.text: This page lists the requirements needed to install Flexygo in a Windows environment with IIS.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before you begin, make sure your environment has:

  • IIS installed and configured (the installer can install it if it isn't)
  • SQL Server 2022 or later (can also optionally be installed from the installer)
  • .NET Hosting Bundle (installed automatically by the installer if its absence is detected)
  • Administrator permissions on the machine

docs.title: Installing IIS and SQL Server
docs.text:
In advanced mode, the installer offers automatic options to:

  • Install IIS if it is not present on the system.
  • Install SQL Server Developer Edition if the user requests it (ideal for test environments or local installations).

docs.title: WebSocket
docs.text:
For Flexygo to work correctly, you must enable WebSocket in the Windows features:

Go to Control Panel → Programs → Turn Windows features on or off and make sure WebSocket is enabled under the IIS features.

docs.title: SQL Server
docs.text:
Flexygo 10 requires SQL Server 2022 or later

Starting with Flexygo 10, the minimum SQL Server version is SQL Server 2022. The application's databases must be on a SQL Server 2022 or later server; if the server is older, upgrade it before installing, updating or migrating the application.

docs.title: Sizing guide
docs.text:
For around 100 simultaneous users, it is recommended to run the application and SQL Server on separate machines:

SQL Server machine Application machine (IIS) Operating system Windows Server 2016 Standard or later Windows Server 2016 Standard or later Processor Intel Xeon (reference: E5-2650 v4 @ 2.20GHz) Intel Xeon (reference: E5-2650 v4 @ 2.20GHz) Memory 16 GB RAM (expandable) 8 GB RAM (expandable) Disk 500 GB 500 GB

Disk space depends on the project; for large-scale document or image management an external NAS is recommended. More users are spread over several application machines behind a load balancer. For databases over 30 GB, see this article on SQL Server memory.

docs.title: Installer: Deployment Mode
docs.text:
The Deployment mode of the Flexygo installer lets you configure the environment for production or pre-production.

Docker in production

For production environments with Docker, we recommend using the Docker guide with a manual docker-compose, which offers greater control over the configuration.

docs.title: 1. Product selection
docs.text:
The first step is choosing which product you want to install. The installer shows the available solutions (Flexygo, SAT, CRM…) and the Custom option, which lets you manually specify the NuGet package to install and its source.

If you select Custom, you must specify the NuGet package name and where to look for it: a remote feed URL or a local physical path. The package name must follow the Flexygo naming convention so that the installer can detect it correctly.

docs.title: 2. Installation mode
docs.text:
Once the product is selected, choose the installation mode according to your environment:

Basic IISAdvanced IISDocker (via Installer)

docs.title: Basic installation
docs.text: Installs Frontend and Backend on the same server and IIS site. Ideal for testing, demos, or small environments.

docs.title: Site configuration
docs.text: Choose the project name, select an existing website or create a new one, set the virtual path (if desired), and the physical directory where the application will be installed.

docs.title: Advanced installation
docs.text: Lets you install Frontend and Backend on different servers, or install only one of the two components. Suitable for customized production installations.

docs.title: Component selection
docs.text: Choose whether to install only Frontend, only Backend, or both. You can also install IIS and/or SQL Server if your environment doesn't have them yet, and choose to install a specific version of the product.

docs.title: Specific version
docs.text: If you selected installing a specific version, specify the package name and its source (remote feed URL or physical path). The wizard will search for the available versions so you can choose the one you need.

docs.title: Frontend configuration
docs.text: Choose the project name, IIS site, virtual path, and physical directory where the Frontend will be installed.

docs.title: Backend configuration
docs.text: Choose the project name, IIS site, virtual path, and physical directory where the Backend will be installed.

docs.title: Docker installation
docs.text:
Deploys Flexygo directly on Docker Desktop. Aimed at demo, testing, or local development environments with containers.

Prerequisite

Make sure you have Docker Desktop installed and running before continuing. You can download it from docker.com/products/docker-desktop.

docs.title: Docker deployment configuration
docs.text:
Configure the container parameters: ports, volumes, and deployment options for Frontend and Backend.

Result

Once the configuration is confirmed, the installer brings up the containers directly in Docker Desktop. You can access the application from Docker Desktop itself or through the configured port.

docs.title: 3. Progress and completion
docs.text:
(Basic IIS and Advanced IIS modes only)

You'll see the installation progress step by step. Once finished, the wizard shows a summary and offers to open the application directly in the browser.

docs.title: Installer: Development Mode
docs.text:
The installer's Development mode is aimed at developers working with Flexygo projects in Visual Studio or VS Code. It offers three operations: creating a new product from the official template, creating an addon (in the products that support them, such as Flexygo), or managing existing products in the workspace.

Prerequisite for VS Code: Node.js in the global PATH

If you're going to work with the project from VS Code, you need Node.js installed and available in the system's global PATH. If it isn't in the PATH, the Frontend build will fail. See the development requirements.

Main screen of Development mode Create productCreate addonManage products

docs.title: Create a new product
docs.text:
This option generates the complete structure of a Flexygo product from the official template: Frontend, Backend, and database projects, ready to open in Visual Studio or VS Code.

Form for creating a new product

Enter the product name and the path where the project will be generated. The installer installs the template (or updates it if already installed) and also installs or updates the development tools:

  • Flexygo Product Tools — lets you generate NuGets and update the project from the command line or from the Visual Studio and VS Code extensions
  • Flexygo MCP — MCP server for building the application with Claude Code and other AI clients

Once completed, it creates the solution from the template.

Product generated — ready to open in Visual Studio or VS Code

Command-line alternative

You can also create a product using the template directly with dotnet new. See the Product Template guide.

docs.title: Create an addon
docs.text:
The Create addon option only appears for the products that support addons, such as Flexygo. It generates an addon solution with the product's addon template: it asks for the product folder and the addon name, which must be different from the product's. If the folder is empty, it creates the product first and then the addon.

The whole process, from creation to packaging as a NuGet, is in Create an addon.

docs.title: Manage existing products
docs.text: This option scans the workspace for Flexygo projects and lets you update the Core version or generate the NuGets for the product.

docs.title: Loading the workspace
docs.text:
On entry, the installer analyzes the workspace looking for Flexygo solutions.

The installer scans the workspace for Flexygo projects

docs.title: Product list
docs.text:
Once loaded, the products are shown with the currently installed version and the latest stable Flexygo version available. You can switch between list and grid view, and filter by name.

List view: current version → latest stable version available, with per-product actions

Grid view with an active filter

docs.title: Updating the Core version
docs.text:
Click Update on the desired product to update the Core NuGet packages to the available version. The installer performs the process and confirms the result.

Confirmation of the product update to the new Core version

Don't update the NuGet packages manually

The updater performs additional steps (resource synchronization, replacing the appsettings while keeping your ConnectionStrings, DatabaseNuget and MailSettings…; see Product management) that do not happen with a manual NuGet update from Visual Studio or VS Code.

docs.title: Generating the product's NuGets
docs.text:
Click Generate NuGets to package the product. The installer asks for the version to tag the generated packages with.

Enter the version with which the product's NuGet packages will be generated

When it completes, the file explorer automatically opens with the folder where the packages were generated. The resulting packages (Frontend, Backend, Conf.Database, Data.Database) are then available to publish to a NuGet feed or distribute to the installer.

docs.title: Flexygo Installer
docs.text:
The Flexygo installer is the main tool for managing the complete lifecycle of an installation: from the initial deployment to migration from previous versions or uninstallation.

Installer home screen (dark mode) Installer home screen (light mode)

docs.title: Available modes
docs.text:
The installer covers the following scenarios:

  • Deployment — Installation for a production or pre-production environment. Available in three variants: basic IIS (single shared site), advanced IIS (independent sites per component), and Docker via the installer.

  • Development — Installation aimed at local development environments, with specific options for working with the source code.

  • Migration — Migration of existing projects or applications from .NET Framework to Flexygo (modern .NET).

  • Uninstall — Clean removal of an existing installation, including its IIS sites and associated databases.

docs.title: Installer: Migration Mode
docs.text:
The installer's Migration mode lets you move projects and applications from .NET Framework to .NET Core (Flexygo). It offers two variants depending on the starting point.

Migration mode offers 2 options

Flexygo 10 requires SQL Server 2022 or later

Starting with Flexygo 10, the minimum SQL Server version is SQL Server 2022. Before migrating, check that the SQL server hosting the application's databases meets this requirement; if it doesn't, upgrade it first. See the System requirements.

Migrate ProductsMigrate Applications

docs.title: Migrate projects
docs.text: This option scans the workspace for Flexygo .NET Framework solutions and lets you migrate them to the Flexygo (modern .NET) structure.

docs.title: Migrate from VS Code with Claude Code
docs.text:
If you open a Flexygo .NET Framework project in VS Code with the Flexygo extension, the panel warns that it uses an outdated version and offers Migrate to Flexygo Core. The window that opens offers two paths:

  • With AI (Claude Code): the extension installs the flexygo-migrar-core skill, which does the whole migration for you: it creates the branch, updates the Flexygo NuGet, runs this installer, places the Core solution in the repository, validates and fixes it, and writes a report, with one commit per phase. Copy the /flexygo-migrar-core command and paste it into Claude Code opened in the project folder, or click Open Claude Code in a terminal.
  • Without AI: download the installer and migrate the project by hand with the steps in this section.

The VS Code extension detects the .NET Framework project and offers to migrate it with the Claude Code skill

docs.title: Loading the workspace
docs.text:
Specify the working folder where the projects are located and click Scan projects. The installer will analyze the workspace looking for Flexygo .NET Framework solutions.

Specify the working folder and click Scan projects

docs.title: Product list
docs.text:
The projects found are shown with their current version. You can switch between list and grid view, and filter by name.

List view with the projects available for migration

Grid view with an active filter

docs.title: Migrate
docs.text: Click Migrate on the desired project. The installer generates the new Flexygo structure from the existing project.

docs.title: Migration completed
docs.text:
When finished, the installer offers to open the migrated project directly in Visual Studio or VS Code.

The migrated project can be opened directly in Visual Studio or VS Code

Checks required after migrating the project

Before building and testing the migrated project, review the following points:

Conf.Database

  • Open the Conf.Database project and review the configuration file and the integrity of the migrated postdeploy script.
  • Also review the staticdata scripts to make sure they were migrated correctly and don't contain obsolete references.
  • Also check the config.sql file and verify its integrity. The migrator automatically replaces AutoUpdatePackageId with AutoUpdatePackageNamespace in this file, but if you have this value configured in any other script you'll need to replace it manually.

Old artifact folders

Manually delete the Properties, obj, and debug folders that may remain from the previous solution in the Frontend, Backend, and Processes (if it exists) projects. These folders can contain .NET Framework assemblies that are incompatible with the new solution. They will be regenerated correctly when building.

Obsolete namespaces in Processes

If the Processes are written in C#, they may use namespaces that no longer exist in modern .NET. The most common cases are:

.NET Framework Namespace .NET Equivalent System.Web Microsoft.AspNetCore.Http System.Web.HttpContext Microsoft.AspNetCore.Http.HttpContext System.Web.HttpRequest Microsoft.AspNetCore.Http.HttpRequest System.Web.HttpResponse Microsoft.AspNetCore.Http.HttpResponse System.Web.HttpServerUtility Microsoft.AspNetCore.Hosting.IWebHostEnvironment System.Web.SessionState Microsoft.AspNetCore.Http.ISession

Review the using statements of each Process and replace the obsolete ones with their equivalents. If there are cases not covered in the table, see the official ASP.NET to ASP.NET Core migration guide.

docs.title: Migrate IIS applications
docs.text: This option detects Flexygo .NET Framework applications deployed in IIS and migrates them to .NET Core in place.

docs.title: Applications found
docs.text:
The installer lists the Flexygo Framework IIS applications detected on the system.

Flexygo Framework applications found in IIS

docs.title: NuGet package source
docs.text:
Before starting, the installer asks for the product's namespace and the URL of the NuGet feed from which it will download the packages corresponding to the application being migrated.

Specify the product namespace and the source NuGet feed

docs.title: Confirmation — Read before continuing
docs.text:
The installer shows a confirmation dialog with important warnings:

Important warnings before starting the migration

Before confirming, keep in mind:

  • The process can take several minutes
  • The application may be affected during the process — it's recommended that no one works on it while the migration is in progress
  • If the application uses custom DLLs, they must be tested after migration to validate they work correctly
  • If you have pending differences between versions to review, do so before continuing — once the application is migrated, they will no longer be available
  • The old Application Pool is NOT stopped or deleted automatically — if other applications share it, you'll need to manage it manually after the migration

The process includes: version validation, database backup and restore, downloading Flexygo .NET Core packages, and updating the IIS application.

docs.title: Progress
docs.text:
The installer shows step-by-step progress, including the backup

Automatic rollback on error

If an error occurs at any point in the process, the installer performs an automatic rollback and leaves the system in exactly its original state. Nothing existing is ever deleted or modified:

  • The application folders are renamed as OLD_<timestamp> — the originals remain intact.
  • The configuration database is likewise renamed as OLD_<timestamp>.
  • If a data database exists, it is also renamed.

It is always possible to return to the previous state manually by restoring the renamed folders and databases.

docs.title: Migration completed
docs.text:
When finished, the installer shows a summary with the IIS sites created (Frontend and Backend) and their physical paths, confirms that the database has been updated to the .NET Core schema, and offers to open the application directly.

Migration summary: IIS sites created, database updated, direct access to the application

Actions required after migration

  • License regenerated — the license is automatically regenerated to keep the same existing license under the new technology. No additional action is needed.
  • All users must log in again — the migration invalidates active sessions.
  • Browser cache reload recommended — since the same site and IIS are kept, the browser may serve previous static files. Reload with Ctrl + Shift + R or clear the cache before using the application.

Next steps

The deployment and update cycle is identical to that of any Flexygo installation. See the Deployment and Update guides for the next steps.

docs.title: Installer: Uninstall Mode
docs.text:
The uninstaller removes a Flexygo application deployed in IIS. It is accessed from the Uninstall button in the bottom-left corner of the installer's main screen.

Access to Uninstall mode from the installer's main screen

docs.title: Available applications
docs.text:
The uninstaller automatically detects all Flexygo applications installed in IIS and shows them in a list. Each application has its own Uninstall button.

List of Flexygo applications found in IIS

docs.title: Confirmation
docs.text:
When you click Uninstall on an application, a confirmation dialog is shown detailing what will be removed:

The installer states exactly what will be removed before proceeding

This action will remove:

  • Applications: Frontend and Backend
  • The IIS sites/applications
  • The Application Pools
  • The configuration database (ConfConnectionString)
  • The physical files on disk

Data databases

Data databases (DataConnectionString and others) are NOT removed automatically. If you want to delete them, do so manually from SQL Server once the uninstallation is complete.

This action cannot be undone

Back up the data database before continuing if you need to keep the application's records.

docs.title: Uninstallation completed
docs.text:
When finished, the installer shows a summary of the removed items.

Confirmation of completed uninstallation with a summary of removed items

Reinstalling after uninstalling

To reinstall Flexygo on the same server, run the installer again in Deployment mode.

docs.title: Reference: appsettings.json
docs.text:
The Backend's appsettings.json file contains all of the application's configuration. The Configuration Wizard automatically manages the main keys; the rest rarely require manual intervention.

In IIS and in a production container, the passwords and keys in this file are stored encrypted: see Encrypted appsettings.

docs.title: Backend — full appsettings.json
Automatically generated keys (Backend)
docs.text:
The first time the application starts, the system generates and persists the following security keys in appsettings.json. The user should not modify them except in very specific scenarios (e.g. key rotation in environments with multiple instances):

Key Purpose JwtSettings.SecretKey Signs the authentication JWT tokens DataProtection.ApplicationId Application identifier for encrypting sensitive data DataProtection.Key Encryption key for ASP.NET Core data protection

These keys do not appear in the file until the first startup and are invisible to the user in the normal installation and configuration flow.

docs.title: Frontend — full appsettings.json
Optional keys (Frontend and Backend)
docs.text:
They are not included in the template and are only added when needed:

Key Purpose ForwardedHeaders.KnownProxies IP addresses of the trusted reverse proxies, so the application accepts the real client IP from them. See Deployment behind a reverse proxy HttpsRedirection (Frontend only) Redirects requests that arrive over http to https. When it is missing, it is true. Set it to false only when a reverse proxy in front already enforces https; see Deployment behind a reverse proxy

docs.title: Automatically generated keys (Frontend)
docs.text:
Just like the Backend, the Frontend generates and persists these keys on first startup. Do not modify except in very specific cases:

Key Purpose JwtSettings.SecretKey Verifies the JWT tokens received from the Backend DataProtection.ApplicationId Identifier for session data encryption DataProtection.Key Encryption key for ASP.NET Core data protection

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
New in version 10.0

Initial setup is now handled by a wizard on the Login screen. Press Empezar to begin. The wizard checks the values and shows progress as it publishes and creates the databases. You can use a dacpac file or a NuGet feed as the schema source.

If you leave or an error occurs, you can return to the first pending step and retry without losing your progress. Credential errors identify the fields to check. If mail is already configured, the wizard skips that step. When setup is complete, press Ir al inicio de sesión.

The Configuration Wizard gets a new installation ready before the first sign-in. It connects the frontend with the backend, creates, updates or reuses the databases, names the project, sets the admin user's password and configures mail. Everything is saved to appsettings.json and to the configuration database, with no need to edit any file by hand.

From web.config to appsettings.json

Unlike .NET Framework applications where the configuration lived in web.config, in Flexygo (based on .NET 9) all configuration is managed through appsettings.json. The wizard takes care of writing and updating this file automatically.

docs.title: Configuration Wizard
docs.text:
The wizard opens automatically when you access the application while the installation is not configured. The start screen sums up what you are going to set up and, under the Start button, shows the Flexygo version and the address of the application.

Wizard start screen

The wizard has five steps, listed on the left with the value saved in each one. Each step checks the data before saving anything. If you leave the wizard, it picks up at the first pending step when you come back.

docs.title: 1. Backend connection
docs.text:
Enter where the backend answers, so the frontend can talk to it:

  • Frontend URL: the public address of the application. The wizard detects it automatically.
  • Backend URL: the address of the backend, with its port. api/backend/ is added when it is saved.

Click Check connection. If the backend answers, Backend reachable appears and, when you click Continue, the URL is saved and the session keys are synced between the frontend and the backend.

Step 1 — The backend has answered

docs.title: 2. Configuration database
docs.text:
This is the database where Flexygo keeps users, permissions and metadata. Enter the SQL Server server, the user, the password and the database name (by convention, {Project}_IC) and click Check.

The wizard checks the server and the database and tells you what it is going to do before doing it:

Situation What the wizard says Button It does not exist It will be created, with the schema of the installed Flexygo version Create database It exists, but from an earlier version An update is available. If it holds real data, back it up first Update and use It exists and is up to date Ready to use: it is used as is Use this database

If you change any value after checking, the wizard checks it again. If the user or the password is wrong, or the database exists but is not a Flexygo configuration database, it says so on the field.

Step 2 — The database does not exist and will be created from the local dacpac

docs.title: Schema source
docs.text:
To create or update the database, the wizard needs its schema. The Schema source box shows where it takes it from:

  • Development · local dacpac: when the application runs from the solution, it uses the dacpac built by the database project. If the project is not built, it offers Build the project; if you changed it after building it, click Rebuild so the dacpac is up to date.
  • Production · NuGet: in an installation, it downloads the database package from the feed configured in DatabaseNuget. If the package is not there, you can Look in another feed (a NuGet v3 feed or a local folder, with a user and token if it asks for them). That feed is only used for this installation: it is not saved to appsettings.json or to the settings.

The configuration database cannot be empty

Without a schema (no dacpac and no package), the wizard does not let you create or update the configuration database. Build the project or enter a feed with the package to continue.

docs.title: Creation or update
docs.text:
When you click the button, the wizard deploys the database and shows each phase: reading the dacpac or downloading the package, creating the database, deploying the schema, loading the data models and saving the connection string. Below it you can see the detail of what is being deployed and the elapsed time.

Do not close the window while it runs. If something fails, the changes are rolled back: click View details to see the error, fix the cause and click Retry.

Step 2 — Progress of the database creation

docs.title: 3. Project and administrator
docs.text:
This step only appears when the configuration database is new. If it already existed, the step is skipped and the project and users it holds are used.

  • Project name: saved to the project settings and to the backend appsettings.json. If the installation already defines it, it is locked.
  • Admin password and Repeat the password: the password of the admin user. It needs at least 8 characters, upper and lower case, a number and a symbol; the list of requirements is ticked as you type. Generate a strong one creates one that meets them.

Click Save and continue.

Step 3 — Project name and administrator password

docs.title: 4. Data databases
docs.text:
The configuration database defines the data connections the product uses. The wizard sets them up one at a time: it says how many there are and which one is next, and the following one appears when the previous one is done.

By default it uses the same server and credentials as the configuration; turn the switch off to enter others. Type the database name and click Check:

Situation What the wizard does It does not exist and there is a schema (dacpac or package) Creates it with the schema of its package It does not exist and there is no schema Creates it empty, with no tables It exists and is from an earlier version Updates it before using it It exists and is up to date Uses it as is

The Schema source works as in step 2, with one difference: without a schema, a data database can be created empty (Create empty database).

AHORA ERP databases

If the connection is to an AHORA ERP database, it must exist: the wizard does not create ERP databases. If it is not found, restore or create it and check again, or fix the name.

Step 4 — The data database does not exist and there is no schema, so it will be created empty

docs.title: 5. Outgoing mail
docs.text:
Flexygo uses this server to recover passwords and send notifications. The step is optional: if you do not have the server yet, click Skip and set it up later. If mail was already configured, the wizard skips this step.

Field Description SMTP server Mail server (for example, smtp.office365.com) Port Usually 587 or 465 Encryption Turn on SSL/TLS if the server requires it Sender Address shown as the sender. It is also set as the email of the admin and guest users SMTP user and SMTP password Account used to authenticate with the server

Click Save and finish.

Step 5 — Outgoing mail server

docs.title: Configuration complete
docs.text:
When it finishes, the wizard shows Flexygo is ready with a summary of what was set up: the backend, the configuration database, the project, each data database and mail. Each one shows what was done (Created, Updated, Existing, Empty, New, Skipped…).

If the application runs on IIS, it is recycled to apply the changes.

Configuration summary

Click Go to sign in. If the project is new, sign in as admin with the password from step 3; if it already existed, with your usual project user.

Application login screen

appsettings.json reference

For a complete reference of the keys available in appsettings.json and their meaning, see Reference: appsettings.json.

docs.title: Encrypted appsettings
docs.text:
In IIS and in a production container, the Backend and Frontend appsettings keep passwords and keys encrypted on disk. Anywhere else (development, Kestrel, the installer's test Docker) they stay in plain text. The application reads them as always: encryption changes nothing about how it is configured or how it works, except that whoever opens the file does not see the secrets.

Encryption is value by value: the rest of the file stays readable and editable.

JSON
"ConnectionStrings": {
  "ConfConnectionString": "enc:v1:Xq3k…",
  "DataConnectionString": "enc:v1:9fTb…"
},
"JwtSettings": {
  "SecretKey": "enc:v1:mW0p…"
},

docs.title: 1. What is encrypted
docs.text:
Value Where it usually is ConnectionStrings:* (every connection string) Backend MailSettings:Password Backend JwtSettings:SecretKey Backend and Frontend DataProtection:Key Backend and Frontend DatabaseNuget:NugetPassword Backend Setup:AdminPassword Backend

Only two files of the conf folder are encrypted: appsettings.json and appsettings.Production.json. The others (appsettings.Development.json, appsettings.local.json…) always stay in plain text; if one holds values encrypted by an earlier version, the application decrypts them when it starts. An empty value is not encrypted.

Each encrypted value starts with enc:v1: (AES-256-GCM). A value that does not start like that is read as it is: you can write one in plain text by hand and the application encrypts it on the next start.

docs.title: 2. Where it is encrypted
docs.text:
Where the application runs decides it; no setting changes it.

Where the application runs Secrets on disk IIS, whether the installer set it up or it was set up by hand Encrypted, always Production Docker container (ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT set to Production or not set) Encrypted Docker set up by the installer for testing (Development environment) Plain text Container with another environment (Development, Staging…) Plain text Kestrel on its own and development (Visual Studio, IIS Express) Plain text
  • Where it is encrypted, the Backend and the Frontend encrypt on start whatever is still in plain text in their conf: a new installation, one coming from a version without encryption, or a value someone wrote by hand. What the product writes itself (the JWT key, the Data Protection key, the mail account set from the panel…) is saved already encrypted.
  • Where it is not, on start they decrypt whatever they find encrypted (for example, a conf copied from an IIS) and say so on the console:
Text Only
appsettings.json: 4 settings decrypted, because this deployment keeps them in plain text (it is neither IIS nor a production container).

Decrypting needs the key the values were encrypted with (section 3); without it the application does not start (section 6).

The Frontend gets its keys with the first page

The Backend generates the JWT and Data Protection keys, and the Frontend gets its copy the first time a page is requested. Until then the Frontend's appsettings may have nothing to encrypt.

docs.title: Who creates it
docs.text:
Nobody, by hand. It is generated at random the first time it is needed on that server or in that volume:

  • on the application's first start in IIS or in a production container;
  • or at the updater's last step in IIS, when updating from a version without encryption (section 5).

The installer never creates it: it only uses it to read the configuration when uninstalling.

docs.title: Where it lives
docs.text:
Where the application runs Where the key is Windows %ProgramData%\Flexygo\keys\config.key, protected with DPAPI at machine level. One per server Docker conf/keys/config.key in the conf volume, with 600 permissions. In production, giving it as a Docker secret or an environment variable is recommended (section 8)

A key given from outside wins over the file, in this order:

  1. The FLEXYGO_CONFIG_KEY variable, with the key in base64 (32 bytes).
  2. The FLEXYGO_CONFIG_KEY_FILE variable, with the path of a file that holds it.
  3. The Docker secret flexygo_config_key (/run/secrets/flexygo_config_key).

A base64 key can be generated, for example, with openssl rand -base64 32.

docs.title: Several applications on the same server
docs.text: On Windows the key belongs to the server, not to each application: every Flexygo application in that IIS shares it. The first one that needs it creates it and the rest use it. That is why a single config export-key covers all of them.

docs.title: Its own key for one application
docs.text:
This is optional. If one application has to carry its own key, set FLEXYGO_CONFIG_KEY only on its IIS application pool, for example with appcmd from an administrator console:

Text Only
%windir%\system32\inetsrv\appcmd.exe set config -section:system.applicationHost/applicationPools /+"[name='MyPool'].environmentVariables.[name='FLEXYGO_CONFIG_KEY',value='<base64 key>']" /commit:apphost
  • Set it before the application encrypts with the server's key, or first run config decrypt (section 7) and let the start encrypt with the new one.
  • That key is written in the IIS configuration (applicationHost.config), not protected with DPAPI.
  • The updater inherits it, because the application itself launches it. The config console does not see it: before using it for that application, set the same variable in the console (set FLEXYGO_CONFIG_KEY=<base64 key>).

docs.title: If it is lost
docs.text:
Without the key nothing can be decrypted

If the key is lost, the encrypted values cannot be recovered: they have to be written again in plain text. When setting up a server, run config export-key (section 7) and keep the file and its password somewhere safe.

docs.title: What it protects and what it does not
docs.text:
• On Windows, DPAPI at machine level means that a copy of the conf or of the key that leaves the server (a backup, a copied folder) cannot be read anywhere else. It does not protect against someone who already controls the server: an administrator, or a program running there, can decrypt just like the application.
  • In Docker, if the key is in the volume, whoever can read the volume (or its copies) has the key and the values. In production, give it as a Docker secret instead.

docs.title: 4. Install and uninstall
docs.text:
• Install in IIS. The installer writes the configuration in plain text, as always, and the application encrypts it on its first start. The Backend ends up with both connection strings and the JWT and Data Protection keys encrypted, and the Frontend with its two keys.
  • The installer's Docker. It is for testing and runs in Development: the configuration stays in plain text.
  • Uninstall. The installer reads the configuration connection string even when it is encrypted, to find the database it has to delete. If this machine cannot decrypt it, it warns and deletes no database.

docs.title: 5. Update and rollback
docs.text:
• Update. The updater reads the encrypted connection strings with the machine's key. If a database name changes during the update, it writes it back encrypted.
  • After updating, in IIS and in a production container the secrets stay encrypted: in IIS the updater leaves the new version's configuration encrypted, and in any case the application encrypts on start whatever it finds in plain text.
  • From a version without encryption. In IIS, the updater encrypts the configuration at the end of the update and creates the server's key if there was none yet. A production container encrypts it on its first start with the new image.
  • A value this machine cannot decrypt stops the update, saying how to fix it: import the key it was encrypted with (Flexygo.Backend.exe config import-key <file> in the application's folder) and update again.
  • Rollback. If the update fails and is undone, the previous version gets its files back as they were, encrypted. Since the key belongs to the machine and not to the version folder, it keeps reading them.

Measured in IIS: after an update whose final step was forced to fail and was rolled back, and after a complete update, both conf folders were still encrypted, with the same key, and the login answered.

docs.title: 6. Moving the application to another server
docs.text:
The Windows key is protected with the machine: copying the config.key file to another server does not work. There are two ways:

  • Take the key. On the old server, config export-key <file> saves it protected with a password. On the new one, config import-key <file> installs it. The copied conf is then read as it is. This only works if the new server has no key yet.
  • Take the configuration in plain text. On the old server, config decrypt. Copy the conf and, on the new one, the application encrypts it on start with that server's key.

The same goes for taking an encrypted conf to a development machine: there the application decrypts it on start, and it needs the key to do so.

If neither is done, the application does not start and says which values it cannot read and the ways out:

Text Only
Some values of the configuration cannot be decrypted on this machine:
  appsettings.json, ConnectionStrings:ConfConnectionString: it was encrypted with another key than the one in C:\ProgramData\Flexygo\keys\config.key (DPAPI, this machine)
Either import the key they were encrypted with ("Flexygo.Backend.exe config import-key <file>", after "Flexygo.Backend.exe config export-key <file>" on the old server), or write those values again in plain text: they are encrypted again on the next start.

docs.title: Moving one application to a server that already runs others
docs.text:
If the destination server already runs Flexygo applications, it already has its key. Do not run import-key --force: it would change the server's key, and the applications already there could no longer read their configuration. Instead:

  1. On the source server, config decrypt in the application's folder.
  2. Copy the application with its conf in plain text.
  3. On the destination, the application encrypts it on start with that server's key.

import-key does not replace a different key that is already there, precisely because whatever that key encrypted would become unreadable. --force does it anyway: use it only if no other application on the server depends on the existing key.

docs.title: 7. The config console
docs.text:
The executable itself has the commands; the .NET SDK is not needed. Run it in the application's folder, from an administrator console (the Windows key is in %ProgramData%):

Text Only
> Flexygo.Backend.exe config
Usage: Flexygo.Backend.exe config <command>
  status                 where the key is and what each appsettings file holds
  decrypt                writes the encrypted values in plain text, to edit them;
                         the next start encrypts them again
  encrypt                encrypts the sensitive values of appsettings.json and appsettings.Production.json now
                         (they stay so in IIS or a production container)
  export-key <file>      saves the key protected with a password, to take it to another server
  import-key <file>      installs a key saved with export-key (--force replaces a different one)
  --password <value>     for export-key and import-key; asked for when missing
Run it in the application's folder, from an administrator console: it needs no SDK.

The Frontend has the same commands (Flexygo.Frontend.exe config …) for its own conf.

docs.title: config status
docs.text:
Where the key is and what each file holds:

Text Only
> Flexygo.Backend.exe config status
Conf: C:\inetpub\flexygo\Backend\conf
Key: C:\ProgramData\Flexygo\keys\config.key (DPAPI, this machine)
appsettings.json: 4 encrypted, 0 sensitive in plain text
appsettings.Development.json: 0 encrypted, 1 sensitive in plain text (always kept in plain text)

If a value cannot be decrypted, it is named under its file with cannot decrypt … and the command ends with code 1.

docs.title: Changing an encrypted value by hand
docs.text:
Text Only
> Flexygo.Backend.exe config decrypt
appsettings.json: 4 decrypted
The application encrypts them again when it starts in IIS or in a production container.

Edit the value in appsettings.json and restart the application (in IIS, recycle the pool): it encrypts it again on start. Without waiting for the start, config encrypt (outside IIS or a production container, the next start decrypts it again):

Text Only
> Flexygo.Backend.exe config encrypt
appsettings.json: 4 encrypted

docs.title: Saving or moving the key
docs.text:
Text Only
> Flexygo.Backend.exe config export-key flexygo-key.txt
Password:
Repeat it:
Key exported to flexygo-key.txt. Keep it, and its password, somewhere safe.

import-key flexygo-key.txt installs it on the other server and shows the resulting status. The password is asked for on the console or given with --password.

docs.title: 8. Docker
docs.text:
A container encrypts its secrets only when its environment is production: ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT set to Production, or not set, which is what ASP.NET assumes by default. With Development (the installer's test Docker) or any other value they stay in plain text.

In the container the commands run with docker exec, through dotnet:

Bash
docker exec <backend-container> dotnet Flexygo.Backend.dll config status
  • The key lives in the conf volume (/app/conf/keys/config.key): recreating the containers or changing the image keeps the key and the configuration. If the volume is deleted, both go together.
  • Environment variables:
Variable What for FLEXYGO_CONFIG_KEY The key in base64. It wins over the one in the volume FLEXYGO_CONFIG_KEY_FILE Path of a file with the key Secret flexygo_config_key The key as a Docker secret, mounted at /run/secrets/flexygo_config_key ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT Production or not set: encrypted. Any other value: plain text

In production, give the key as a Docker secret:

YAML
services:
  flx-backend:
    image: flexygo-backend
    environment:
      - ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT=Production
    secrets:
      - flexygo_config_key
  flx-frontend:
    image: flexygo-frontend
    environment:
      - ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT=Production
    secrets:
      - flexygo_config_key
secrets:
  flexygo_config_key:
    file: ./flexygo_config_key.txt

Create the file before the first docker compose up, with a new base64 key:

Bash
openssl rand -base64 32 > flexygo_config_key.txt
  • Every container gets the same secret: the frontend and the backend, and each replica if there are several. A replica with another key cannot read what the others encrypted.
  • If the file is missing, the application does not start. Docker does not warn: it creates an empty folder with that name instead and mounts it as the secret. The application notices, does not start and says why in the container's log (docker compose logs); it never encrypts with a key of its own. To fix it: docker compose down, delete that folder, create the file and start again. The same happens when the file is empty, or when FLEXYGO_CONFIG_KEY_FILE points to something that is not a file holding the key.
  • The secret must hold the key in plain base64. The file config export-key writes cannot be used directly, because it is protected with a password.
  • The installer's test Docker (Development) does not encrypt and does not get the secret.

Give the key from the start

If the key is passed by variable or secret after the application has encrypted with the volume's key, the values already encrypted cannot be read. Pass it from the first start, or before changing it run config decrypt and let the start encrypt again with the new one.

MSSQL_SA_PASSWORD and the encrypted string

The Backend container's start replaces Password= in appsettings.json with the value of MSSQL_SA_PASSWORD. In a production container, with the string already encrypted, it does not find it, so changing that variable no longer changes the password. To change it: config decrypt inside the container, edit the string in the volume and restart.

docs.title: 1) Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Settings table (in the configuration database) with:
    • AutoUpdateURL — URL of the NuGet feed (e.g. https://nuget.ahorabh.com/v3/index.json).
    • AutoUpdatePackageNamespace — Product namespace that identifies all the nugets (e.g. from CRMCORE.Conf.Database it would be CRMCORE).
    • AutoUpdateBeta — 0/1 to allow prerelease versions.

  • DbConnectionStrings table (in the configuration database) with:

    • ConnStringId (e.g. ConfConnectionString / DataConnectionString)
    • PackageDbName without the ProductName prefix or the Database suffix, just the middle part (e.g. Conf); the rest is concatenated with the AutoUpdatePackageNamespace setting and .Database.
    • Active = 1 and UpdateDataModel = 1 for the connections that must be updated.

  • Docker Compose:

    • In backend:
    • If using a NuGet repository with credentials, use the NUGET_USER and NUGET_PASSWORD variables.
    • FLEXYGO_PACKAGES_ROOT variable pointing to the same path created in the backend's Dockerfile (e.g. /var/lib/flexygo/packages).
    • Healthcheck so the frontend waits until the backend is ready: - The backend container must have curl installed. - The health route must exist and return 200 (see the example in point 2).
    • In frontend:
      • MAINT_TOKEN variable (the token that will be requested for the update).
      • depends_on on the frontend pointing to the backend with condition: service_healthy.

Note: create the packages folder in the backend's Dockerfile, with write permissions for the user running the app:

Docker
RUN mkdir -p /var/lib/flexygo/packages \
 && chown -R 1000:1000 /var/lib/flexygo

If you use a healthcheck with curl, install it:

Docker
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

docs.title: 2) Example docker-compose.yml
docs.text:
YAML
services:
  flx-frontend:
    image: flexygo-frontend
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      - ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT=Production
      - MAINT_TOKEN=${MAINT_TOKEN}
    secrets:
      - flexygo_config_key
    ports:
      - "${FRONTEND_PORT}:8080"
    volumes:
      - flx-front-conf:/app/conf
      - flx-front-custom:/app/custom
    networks:
      - flx-front-network
    depends_on:
      flx-backend:
        condition: service_healthy

  flx-backend:
    image: flexygo-backend
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      - ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT=Production
      - FLEXYGO_PACKAGES_ROOT=/var/lib/flexygo/packages
    secrets:
      - flexygo_config_key
    volumes:
      - flx-back-conf:/app/conf
      - flx-back-custom:/app/custom
    networks:
      - flx-front-network
      - flx-back-network
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "curl -fsS http://flx-backend:8080/api/backend/Sys/ApplicationStatus || exit 1"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 10
      start_period: 3s
networks:
  flx-front-network:
    driver: bridge
  flx-back-network:
    driver: bridge
volumes:
    flx-front-conf:
    flx-front-custom:
    flx-back-conf:
    flx-back-custom:
secrets:
  flexygo_config_key:
    file: ./flexygo_config_key.txt

With ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT=Production the containers keep the passwords and keys of their appsettings encrypted. The flexygo_config_key secret gives them the key: create the flexygo_config_key.txt file before the first docker compose up (openssl rand -base64 32 > flexygo_config_key.txt) and keep it safe. The details are in Encrypted appsettings.

docs.title: 3) Behavior when bringing up a new version
docs.text:
• Run docker compose up -d with the new image.
  • If the app version > the DB version, the frontend automatically enters maintenance mode.

docs.title: 4) Update process
docs.text:
1. Go to /maintenance/update.
  2. Enter the MAINT_TOKEN (same value as in the frontend's compose).
  3. On confirming:
    • The DbConnectionStrings connections with Active = 1 and UpdateDataModel = 1 are read.
    • The NuGet package is downloaded (using FLEXYGO_PACKAGES_ROOT).
    • The updates for all marked DBs are applied.
  4. When finished:
    • Maintenance mode is disabled.
    • The user is redirected to the login page.

docs.title: DbConnectionStrings
docs.text:
• PackageDbName correct: only the middle part, without the namespace or .Database (e.g. Conf)
  • Active = 1 and UpdateDataModel = 1

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
• AutoUpdateURL valid and reachable from the containers
  • AutoUpdateNugetUser / AutoUpdateNugetPassword defined if the feed requires credentials
  • AutoUpdateBeta set according to whether you need prerelease

docs.title: FLEXYGO_PACKAGES_ROOT
docs.text: • Exists and is writable in the backend container

docs.title: MAINT_TOKEN
docs.text: • Defined in the frontend and matches the one entered at /maintenance/update

docs.title: Flexygo Updater
docs.text:
New in version 10.0

In Version management, you can review what each version includes and use Update to start a wizard that can also revert the application or switch it to another version. Before continuing, the wizard checks the requirements and shows progress step by step, with Flexygo tips. When it finishes, it displays the result, the time taken and the version it started from. Select Show log to view the detailed log.

Other administrators can follow an operation in progress. Each update or removal keeps its result and log. Administrators only can access this feature.

The Flexygo updater lets you update the version of the deployed application without having to reinstall from scratch. The process coordinates the Frontend and Backend to validate, download, and apply the new version, automatically performing the necessary backups and configuration changes.

docs.title: Update flow
docs.text:
Below is the complete flow of the Flexygo update process:

flowchart TD
    A[User clicks 'Update version' in Flexygo] --> B{Are Front and Back on the same server?}
    B -- Yes --> C[Backend updates its Updater and the Frontend's]
    B -- No --> D[Backend notifies Frontend to update its Updater]
    C --> E[Frontend and Backend Updaters notify their applications]
    D --> E
    E --> F[Frontend and Backend validate requirements]
    F --> G{Validations correct?}
    G -- No --> H[Show error and stop the process]
    G -- Yes --> I[Download and prepare NuGets for the new version]
    I --> J{Application to update}
    J -- Frontend --> K[Copy new content and customizations]
    J -- Backend --> L[Copy content, customizations, back up DB, and apply DACPAC]
    K & L --> M[Final step: IIS configuration, rename app and DB, merge appsettings]
    M --> N[Application ready on the new version]

Summary

As shown in the diagram above, the Flexygo update process coordinates Frontend and Backend to validate, download, and prepare the new version, perform the necessary backups, and finish by updating files, the database, and the configuration — ensuring a fast and secure update.

Application Pool permissions

If the updater cannot overwrite files during the update process, make sure the IIS Application Pool user has write permissions on the destination folder. Without these permissions, the update process will fail when trying to replace the application's files.

Permissions to stop processes

In addition to write permissions, the Application Pool user needs permissions to stop processes (kill process) during the update. Without these permissions, the updater will not be able to stop the running application before replacing the binary files.

To update dockerized applications, see Update in Docker Containers.

docs.title: What to check when updating 10.0+
docs.text:
Version 10 brings many new features that change nothing of what you already had: they are in the release notes. This page gathers the opposite: what already existed and now works differently, and what is worth checking before or right after updating an application.

It is ordered by who notices it. If you only have a minute, start with the checklist.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text: Check If… ☐ SQL Server 2022 or later the SQL server is older than SQL Server 2022 ☐ Process calls through the WebAPI you have integrations that run processes with /webapi/exec ☐ Columns an integration reads an integration reads columns that are not properties of the object ☐ Reverse proxy and IP lockout the application is behind a proxy or a load balancer ☐ Your own administration pages you created pages that only an administrator should see ☐ Your own style sheets, interface and logo you are going to move users from flexy2022 to skin2026 ☐ Your own code on calendars, forms or icons your product has custom JavaScript or CSS

docs.title: An object's processes are called with their object
docs.text:
A process defined on an object always runs through that object: POST /webapi/exec/{Process}/{Object}/{id}, or POST /webapi/exec/{Process}/{Object}?filter=… for the collection. Called without the object, it answers 400; so does a collection without filter. Processes that hang from no object are called as before.

Refusals now have their own status (403 for the role, 404 if the record does not exist, 409 if its state does not allow it) instead of a 500 or a 200 with the error inside. The details and the "before and now" table are in WebAPI security.

If you generate the client from the OpenAPI

Each token's OpenAPI only announces what its role can see or run, paging starts at 0 and the operations have their own names. Regenerate the client after updating.

docs.title: Only the defined properties are served
docs.text:
The WebAPI_OnlyDefinedProperties setting comes on (also when it is missing from the settings table): the WebAPI and the MCP server return only the object's defined properties and its keys, in lists, records, insert schemas and the OpenAPI. Before, they returned every column of the table, property or not.

If an integration reads a column that is not a property, define it as a property of the object or, if there is no other way, set the option to false.

docs.title: IP lockout after failed token attempts
docs.text:
50 failed POST /token attempts in 60 seconds from the same address lock it out, in the whole application (sign-in page included) and with no end date: it stays locked until an administrator removes the row in IP Lockouts. A user that does not exist, a wrong password and an invalid refresh_token count. Every failure is written to the WebAPI log.

Setting Default 0 WebAPI_MaxFailedTokenAttempts 50 turns the lockout off WebAPI_FailedTokenInterval 60 (seconds) turns the lockout off

Behind a proxy, declare the proxy

If the application is behind a reverse proxy or a load balancer that is not in ForwardedHeaders:KnownProxies, every request arrives with the proxy's IP: an integration with an expired password locks out every user. Configure it as explained in Deployment behind a reverse proxy.

And if the Frontend and the Backend are on different machines, both need the same JwtSettings:SecretKey: the Frontend uses it to sign the client's real IP.

docs.title: Other changes an integrator notices
docs.text:
• Validated filters. A filter with comments (--), ; or unclosed brackets or quotes answers 400. A role's collection filter always applies to the rows; if it cannot be applied, the request fails instead of being served unfiltered.
  • Dates. Inserts and edits through the WebAPI read and write the date as it is stored in the database, with no time-zone conversion. GET /webapi/context gives the server's time zone (serverTimeZone, serverUtcOffset). Check the clients that compensated for the time zone.
  • OnChange processes. On an insert through the WebAPI, a property's change process runs even if the property has no dependents.
  • Licence. The WebAPI's data operations require a valid licence.

docs.title: Node security and page security
docs.text: The security of a menu node only decides whether the shortcut is shown: the page it opens can still be opened by typing its address. For one of your administration pages to be seen by nobody else, set page security as well (allUsers without permission). Administrators and designers bypass that check.

docs.title: Screens for administrators only
docs.text: Change profile in the user menu is only shown to administrators, and develop mode only to designer roles. The global search over system objects (objects, pages, processes…) is only offered to administrators and designers: what a regular user should search for is configured in their searches.

docs.title: Process security
docs.text:
An object-and-process rule on an object the process is not linked to stops applying: the process's general rule is used.

The general rules are new: they are set per process (by role, user or faculty) and also protect the processes that hang from no object. Without general rules, each process behaves as before.

docs.title: Other changes
docs.text:
• Role and permission changes apply within a few seconds, without the user signing in again.
  • The after-sign-in process (AfterLoginProcess) runs only once and, if it fails, the user still gets in and sees the error. If you relied on it to stop the sign-in, review it.
  • Account lockout: it is configured with UserLockoutMaxFailedAttempts and UserLockoutMinutes (5 and 5). The user's LockoutEndDateUtc property is renamed LockoutEnd: change it in your templates or code.
  • Live notices of inserts and changes: an object with InsertTriggerEvent, UpdateTriggerEvent or DeleteTriggerEvent turned on starts notifying; before, those columns had no effect.
  • A module security condition that fails no longer leaves the page blank: the module is hidden and the error is written to the log.

docs.title: 3. Configuration and deployment
docs.text:
What Now What to do SQL server The minimum requirement is SQL Server 2022 or later Update the SQL server before updating the application. See System requirements Configuration file appsettings.{Environment}.json is loaded; appsettings.Development.json is not published Check which file holds your configuration Updater packages In C:\ProgramData\Flexygo\Packages (FLEXYGO_PACKAGES_ROOT wins if it exists) Permissions and space on the new path Maintenance mode It is turned on from the application's panel and keeps everyone out except the administrator who turned it on. The system processes EnableMaintenanceMode and DisableMaintenanceMode are withdrawn If you called them from a button or an integration, use the panel Upload size Up to 2 GB in Kestrel, IIS and web.config Check the proxy's limit, if there is one Static resources Compressed and with long caching; the address changes with the content Check the cache of a CDN or proxy News on the sign-in page They are fetched from an external service Without internet access, set DisableNews to true

New scheduled tasks. The update adds three tasks that start on their own:

  • Webhook sending (flxWebhookDispatcher, every minute): sends the pending notices to external systems and retries those that failed. It only does something if you have set up outbound webhooks.
  • Task escalation (flxTaskEscalation, every 5 minutes): approval tasks that go past their deadline are escalated to the person named; if they name no one, they expire.
  • Health watch (HealthWatch, every 15 minutes): checks the same as the health panel (machine, SQL Server, databases, backups, Frontend…) and, if something is in alarm or warning, notifies the administrators in the bell.
