Pay special attention to the Backend entry: the src path must point to the same folder you configured as OutputPath in step 2. If your addon includes static assets (JS, CSS, images), uncomment the Frontend entry — otherwise nuget pack will fail if those files don't exist.

With the module.json and .nuspec ready, generate the addon's NuGet package following the process described in Packaging addons.

docs.title: Try it: from installed application to a project that builds and runs 10.0+
Try it: from installed application to a project that builds and runs 10.0+
docs.text:
Here an application built by hand on top of the core becomes a .NET project from the product template: you export it from the control panel, build it on your machine, publish its two databases and run it. In the end you have the same application —menus, pages, objects, processes and the master data you choose— running from a project that can now be pushed to a repository and taken to continuous integration.

What travels and what doesn't, every option in the window and every server step are in the reference: Export the application as a project.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text: A version 10 application with your project's origin active What travels is what belongs to the active origin (for example, 2 · Project). What was created with origin 0 active is indistinguishable from the core and does not travel. An administrator user Only administrators use the window. On the server: access to the updater's NuGet feed The export installs the product's template ({Namespace}.Product.Template, from the AutoUpdatePackageNamespace setting; Flexygo.Product.Template for Flexygo) of the same version as the application. If there is no .NET SDK, it downloads it the first time. On your machine: .NET SDK, SQL Server and sqlpackage To build, publish the databases and run. And access to the same NuGet feeds (the project's nuget.config).

docs.title: 1. Open the window and read the preview
docs.text:
Control panel → action list → Export as project. The window reads the installation and says what it is going to take.

Check:

  • The configuration of origin N: the origin is your project's, not 0 (with 0 the window says so and does not allow exporting).
  • The data model: the connection of your tables (those marked with Update data model in Connection strings). If it says none marked, the project will carry an empty data project.
  • The custom folder: expand Choose what travels and look at which folders and files of custom will travel. The document and image repositories, the run-time folders and anything over 100 MB come unticked; untick too whatever is data and not project (the custom folder).
  • .NET SDK found and the template for your application's version (already installed, or that it will be downloaded).

docs.title: 2. Choose the master data
docs.text: Expand Choose the tables that travel with their rows. The catalogs come checked (small tables that others point to: statuses, types, categories): without their rows nothing could be created in the project. Also check whatever you need for testing. If you check a large table, or one that points to another that does not travel, the window warns in yellow; it does not prevent exporting.

docs.title: 3. Export
docs.text:
Type the Product name (letters, digits and underscore; it names the solution and each project: SalesExamples.Backend, SalesExamples.Conf.Database…), leave Scripts travel as origin at 1 · Product and click Export.

The window shows the steps with their time and, when finished, downloads the zip.

Check: exported, all steps in green (or in yellow with their reason in Worth a look) and a zip of a few MB. In a small application it takes one or two minutes; the first time somewhat longer, because it installs the template.

docs.title: 4. Build it on your machine
docs.text:
Unzip the file and, in its folder:

Bash
dotnet build SalesExamples.sln

Check: Build succeeded, 0 errors. The first time it takes several minutes, because it downloads the template packages.

docs.title: 5. Publish both databases from scratch
docs.text:
The README.md at the root of the zip has both commands already written with your product name:

Bash
sqlpackage /a:Publish /sf:SalesExamples.Conf.Database\bin\Debug\SalesExamples.Conf.Database.dacpac /tsn:<server> /tdn:SalesExamples_Conf /tu:<user> /tp:<password> /ttsc:True /p:IncludeCompositeObjects=True /v:ProjectName=SalesExamples /v:OriginDatabaseName=NULL /v:CurrentDacVersion=1.0.0.0
sqlpackage /a:Publish /sf:SalesExamples.Data.Database\bin\Debug\SalesExamples.Data.Database.dacpac /tsn:<server> /tdn:SalesExamples_Data /tu:<user> /tp:<password> /ttsc:True

Check: Successfully published database in both. The configuration database has the core plus your configuration (as origin 1), and the data database, your tables with the master data rows.

docs.title: 6. Run it
docs.text:
In SalesExamples.Backend\conf\appsettings.Development.json:

  • ConfConnectionString and DataConnectionString, pointing to the two databases you have just published;
  • MailSettings.Configured set to true (a new installation waits for mail to be configured on its first start);
  • and, if you are going to have the original application open at the same time, other ports (also in the Frontend's appsettings.Development.json).

Start Backend and Frontend together (the SalesExamples.slnLaunch.user profile in Visual Studio) and log in with your user.

Check: the same menu, the same pages and lists, the same objects and the same settings you changed (the AI assistant or the web API turned on, the application description) as in the source application. And create a record in a table that depends on a catalog: if it saves, the master data have travelled correctly.

docs.title: 7. Republish it
docs.text: Publish the databases again on top, without deleting them (increase CurrentDacVersion in the configuration one). The MERGE scripts insert and update, and never delete: the record you created is still there. This is what will happen on every product update.

docs.title: If something goes wrong
docs.text: What you see Why What to do The window does not allow exporting and mentions origin 0 The active origin is the core's Activate the project's origin and reopen the window The template step comes out in yellow, or with another version The feed does not have your application's version (happens with development versions of the core) The configuration may fail to publish in step 5: use an application of a released version The configuration database does not publish and names a column The installed template is of a different version than the application The same: the application version and the package version must match Creating a record fails with "It would generate duplicates" A row that a foreign key points to is missing (a catalog or a record, such as the administrator's employee) Check that table in step 2 and export again The data project comes out empty No connection marked with Update data model Mark it in Connection strings, or leave the project without tables A setting you had changed in the application is missing Changed settings travel as UPDATE at the end of config.sql, except environment ones: those of the updater, telemetry, paths, passwords and integrations with credentials (Azure, Google, Office, payments…) Put it in the project's config.sql, or in each installation if it is an environment one

docs.title: Export the application as a project 10.0+
Export the application as a project 10.0+
docs.text:
New in version 10.0

The export assistant shows the selected template and version, explains what will be included, and lets you follow the progress until the ZIP downloads. You can choose custom files and folders and modify the template. By default, it uses the installed product’s template and excludes the document and image repositories and other large files. It supports projects larger than 2 GB and checks that there is enough disk space. It also records exports and errors.

Users are not included in the export, and secrets are kept in a local file that is not shared. If the active origin is reserved, the assistant warns you and suggests the first available destination. Only authorized administrators can use it.

A Flexygo application can start out configured by hand on top of the core —objects, pages, processes, style sheets— without any project behind it. When that application grows and it needs to be developed and maintained with continuous integration, Export as project turns it into a project of the product template: the same solution that dotnet new flexygoproduct generates, with the installation's configuration, data model, static files and DLLs already inside, in a zip ready to open with Visual Studio and push to a repository.

Want to do it end to end with an application of your own? Try it: from installed application to a project that builds and runs.

What it is and what it isn't

The export generates the project; it does not build or publish anything on the server. Building, publishing the databases and running the product is the developer's job, on their machine, as described in Create a product with Flexygo. The application it is exported from does not change: neither its data, nor its origins, nor its files.

docs.title: 1. Before exporting: an origin of your own
docs.text:
Everything that belongs to the project has to be in an origin other than 0, which is the core. The configuration rows of the active origin are exported (the one shown in the control panel, Active origin, and in which the team has built the application); what was created with the active origin at 0 cannot be told apart from the core and does not travel.

With the active origin at 0 the window says so and does not allow exporting:

With origin 0 active: "Nothing of the core is exported". Activate the project's origin and reopen the window

The target origin: 1 for a product, 2 for the child of a product

In the project scripts the rows travel with the target origin chosen in the window, not with the active one. A product born from the core goes as 1 (Product): the template post-deploy leaves each installation working in 2 (Project), so a product whose MERGE scripts were origin 2 would delete the customer's customizations on every update. A product that is the child of another product (its parent already takes 1) goes as 2, and so on. The conversion is done only in the scripts: the application keeps its active origin. 0 is not offered as a target.

docs.title: 2. Where it is
docs.text:
In the control panel, in the action list: Export as project (the folder-with-arrow icon). It opens its own window that carries the export from start to finish: what is going to be done, the steps while it runs and the result.

  • Only administrators use it.
  • One export at a time per installation. If one is running, the window says who launched it and at what time, and offers Follow it to follow it.

docs.title: 3. What it shows before starting
docs.text:
As soon as it opens, the window reads the installation and says what it is going to take. The lines change with what is chosen: the target origin and what is ticked in the custom folder (3.1).

The preview with origin 2 active and the CRMCore product: the configuration that travels, the data model, the static files, the custom folder, the DLLs, the SDK and the template Line What it says The configuration of origin N How many rows from how many tables travel as MERGE scripts of the Conf.Database project: those of the active origin plus those already in the target one. And, if any, how many rows from other origins are left out and from which tables The data model Which connections take their schema to the project and which project each one goes to (4), or none marked if there are none Static files How many CSS and JS files the origin registers, and how many of them are not on disk The custom folder How many folders and files of the Frontend's custom folder travel, out of how many, with their size, and how much is left out; or that the Frontend has no custom folder (3.1) Process DLLs How many process DLLs of the origin are not from the core, how many are not in bin and how many belong to an addon (only listed) .NET SDK Whether the server has an SDK (found, with the version) or not (not on this server: the first export downloads it into a private Backend folder, without administrator permissions; it needs internet and takes a few more minutes). And the template: whether it is already installed and in which version, or that it will be downloaded from the updater's feed the first time

Below, what is requested:

Field What it is Product name .NET identifier (letters, digits and underscore, starting with a letter). It names the solution and each project: CRMCore.Backend, CRMCore.Conf.Database… Scripts travel as origin The target origin (1). 1 · Product by default Template package and Template short name The template the project is generated on. They are worked out from the product's namespace (AutoUpdatePackageNamespace): Flexygo.Product.Template and flexygoproduct for Flexygo. They can only be changed by turning on Custom template, to generate the project on another product's template

The static files and the DLLs always travel, because the rows that name them travel and without them the project would point to nothing:

  • Static files: the files the origin registers in Skins_Css, Plugins and Interfaces_Types_JS, copied under the project Frontend's wwwroot at the same path (~/crm/css/crm.css → wwwroot/crm/css/crm.css), so the rows remain valid as they are.
  • Process DLLs: the DLLs that the origin's processes run and that are not from the core, as a binary reference of the Processes project (7).

Export is enabled when the name is valid, the active origin is not 0 and no other export is running. At the bottom, a reminder: nothing is built here; the zip is for a developer's machine.

docs.title: 3.1 The custom folder: choosing what travels
docs.text:
The Frontend's wwwroot/custom folder usually mixes project (your own JS, CSS and images) with data (what people attach, photos, exports). That is why it does not travel in full: Choose what travels expands its top-level folders and files, with how many files each one holds and its size, a search box and two shortcuts, Suggested (what comes ticked by default) and None. Only what is ticked travels, copied as it is.

What is data or weighs a lot comes unticked, with its reason

These come unticked by default, with a label that says why:

Label What it is documents / images The folders where the configuration keeps documents or images (the paths of the objects' document and image managers), whatever they are called run time Those the installation writes while it runs: images, documents, avatars, temp and Scripting Left out for its size Any folder or file over 100 MB. If it is ticked, its row warns and the line counts the large ones that travel; the list opens by itself when there is one

The preview line sums up the choice (for example, 1 of 8 folders, 3 of 3 files · 1 KB and 176.9 MB left out). Every time the window opens it is proposed again with these rules: the choice is not saved.

docs.title: 4. The data model is decided by the connections
docs.text:
There is no longer an "include the data model" option in the window. The schema (tables, views, procedures, functions, types and triggers) of the active connections marked to update their data model travels: the same mark the updater uses to know which databases it has to update. The configuration connection never counts, and an ERP database is not marked, so it does not travel.

Where each one goes is given by its package name (PackageDbName):

Marked connection Project With PackageDbName = Data {Product}.Data.Database, the template's data project With another name, for example Crm {Product}.Crm.Database: a copy of the data project added to the solution, under the Database folder. The report warns that the template's pipelines and Docker files only build Data.Database: the others have to be added by hand None marked {Product}.Data.Database is left empty and the report says so (an application on top of an ERP, or with its tables created by script). If the product has no tables of its own, it is removed as explained in the template's DOCKER.md

A marked connection is skipped, and the report says so, if its PackageDbName is not valid as a project name, if the installation does not have its connection string, if it points to the configuration database itself or if another marked one already takes the same project.

docs.title: 4.1 Master data: the tables that travel with their rows
docs.text:
The schema alone is not enough for the project to work: tables usually have required foreign keys to catalogs (statuses, types, categories), and without their rows nothing can be created. That is why, under The data model, Choose the tables that travel with their rows expands the tables of each marked connection with their rows, a search box and two shortcuts, Catalogs only and None. The section line says how many tables and rows travel, and how many warnings there are.

The catalogs come checked; the rest are checked by hand
  • The catalogs come checked: small tables (up to 500 rows, with a primary key) that others point to and that point to none. The window explains this under the title, and the catalog tag repeats it on hover. Every time the window opens, the proposal is made again with that rule: the choice is not saved.
  • Each chosen table travels as a MERGE without delete in scripts\post\<table>.sql of the data project, in the order of its foreign keys, from the template post-deploy. Publishing the project adds and updates those rows; it does not delete the ones the target database already has.
  • Warnings, which do not stop the export and turn the Data model step yellow: a table that points to another that does not travel (publishing will reject it unless the database already has those rows), a table without a key, one with more than 500 rows, or a database user that cannot create procedures (then the project travels without rows). An empty table is left out.
  • The README.md at the root of the zip lists the master data tables, and the action log stores them with their rows.

docs.title: 5. While it runs
docs.text:
When you click Export the window switches to the steps: at the top "Step N of 10" with a bar and the time, and each step with its time and a line of what it has done. The Show log switch shows the output of dotnet and of each operation.

Step What it does 1. Origin Checks the name and the origins, and counts the rows per table 2. .NET SDK Looks for the SDK on the server and, if there is none, installs it once in a private Backend folder 3. Product template Installs the product's template, {Namespace}.Product.Template from its AutoUpdatePackageNamespace (Flexygo.Product.Template for Flexygo), or the one chosen with Custom template, from the same feed and with the same credentials as the updater, in the application's version; if the feed does not have it, the highest one below it (the step says which one it used), and otherwise the latest. It does not download it again while it is the same. If the feed does not respond and one was installed before, it uses that one and the step comes out yellow 4. Solution Generates the solution with dotnet new flexygoproduct, the same template a developer or TeamCity uses 5. Configuration scripts One MERGE per table, like those of Generate scripts, in scripts\staticdata of Conf.Database, referenced from the post-deploy. And the settings the installation changed with respect to the core, as UPDATE at the end of scripts\config.sql (see 9) 6. Data model The schema of each marked connection (4), one line per connection with the objects it carries 7. Static files Copies the registered static files 8. Custom folder Copies what is ticked in the custom folder (3.1) 9. Process DLLs Copies the non-core DLLs to Processes\lib and references them from the .csproj 10. Zip and download Checks that the zip fits on the server's disk, writes it to disk (without bin, obj or .vs) and downloads it

If nothing in the custom folder is ticked, step 8 comes out as skipped. There is no cancel button: closing the window while it runs asks first, because the export continues on the server and the zip can only be collected by reopening the window before it finishes (and clicking Follow it).

docs.title: 6. When it finishes
docs.text:
If it succeeds, the zip downloads by itself and the window keeps what deserves attention:

  • the name and size of the zip, and Download again;
  • Worth a look: first what has to be fixed (registered files that were not on disk, DLLs that were not in bin, marked connections that were not exported…) and then what is worth knowing (the empty data model, the DLLs that travel without source code…);
  • the steps, with the first four summarised in one line when everything went well;
  • The full report, collapsible, with everything that was done and everything that was left out, table by table.

The export and its zip are kept for one hour on the server; after that they are deleted automatically and Download again no longer works: export again.

Before writing the zip, the free space is checked: if it does not fit, the export stops with a message that says how much the project takes and how much free space that disk has left. Free some space and export again.

If it fails, the window says "… could not be exported" and "Stopped at step N of 10 · nothing was downloaded, nothing changed": the failed step comes out in red with the error, the log opens by itself, Copy details copies the error and the log to pass them on to whoever is responsible, and Try again goes back to the preview.

docs.title: 7. DLLs without source code
docs.text:
A process can run a separately compiled DLL (Processes.File outside ~/bin/flx*.dll). The exported project carries it in Processes\lib\ and references it as a binary, so that it builds and works like the installation; lib\README.md lists each one. They are a debt of the project: the team should replace each reference with its source code as soon as it has it. A DLL with the same name as the project's own Processes assembly is not referenced (it would clash with it): it is copied and noted.

The DLLs of an addon (~/custom/<addon>/) do not belong to the project: they are listed and not copied; the addon is installed in the target application.

docs.title: 8. What to do with the zip
docs.text:
1. Unzip it and open the solution with Visual Studio (or dotnet build).
  2. Publish the databases from their .sqlproj projects (development installation).
  3. Configure the Backend's appsettings.json: the template leaves it with empty connection strings and the product's PackageId.
  4. Push it to a repository and continue with product management and continuous integration.

The template version and the core version must match

The project references the Flexygo.* packages of the version of the template that was installed (the application's). If the application is ahead of any published package —which only happens in a core development environment—, the exported configuration database will not publish until the package for that version exists.

docs.title: 9. What does not travel
docs.text:
• Rows created with the active origin at 0 (indistinguishable from the core) and those of other origins different from the active and the target ones: the preview and the report count them per table.
  • The data in the databases, except the tables chosen as master data (4.1): for the rest, only the schema, and only that of the marked connections (4).
  • Environment settings: the settings the installation changed travel as UPDATE in config.sql (the MCP or the web API turned on, ApplicationDescription…), but not those that belong to each installation: password-type settings, those of the updater (flx-version), telemetry, paths and integrations with credentials (flx-azure, flx-google, flx-office, flx-payments, flx-passbook, flx-clave, flx-sendinblue, flx-abh), nor BundleGUID. The window lists in Worth a look those that travel.
  • Whatever is left unticked in the custom folder (3.1). By default: the document and image repositories, the run-time folders (images, documents, avatars, temp, Scripting) and anything over 100 MB.
  • A file that a row registers and is not on disk: the row travels and the report warns about it.
  • A DLL that a process names and is not in bin: the process travels and the report warns about it.

Frontend and Backend on different servers

The export runs in the Backend. The DLLs are there; the Frontend files (the registered ones and the custom folder) are requested from the Frontend through its internal file API. There is no need to share folders or copy anything by hand. In that case the preview cannot check one by one which static files are missing: the report says so when it finishes. And the zip, which the Backend hands over to the Frontend, can be at most 700 MB: if it is larger, the export says so and you export again with fewer files from custom.

docs.title: MCP server prerequisites
docs.text: Make sure you have the project's general requirements covered before continuing. In addition, the MCP server has its own extra requirements.

docs.title: .NET 10 SDK
docs.text:
The MCP server is distributed as a global dotnet tool and is installed automatically when creating a new product from the installer or when migrating a Flexygo Framework project. For that automatic installation to work, the team must already have the .NET 10 SDK installed.

Download it from the official page: 👉 https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download

Verify that it's installed:

Bash
dotnet --list-sdks

docs.title: Claude Code
docs.text:
The server is used from Claude Code, in any of its forms: the desktop app, the VS Code extension or the terminal. The /flx-* commands of the workflow and the Flexygo panel belong to Claude Code.

Other MCP clients can use the server's tools, but without the commands or the panel.

docs.title: Configured connection strings
docs.text:
Blocking requirement

The flexygo-mcp server needs access to the project's databases in order to operate. If the Backend's appsettings.json doesn't have the connection strings configured, the server will start but won't be able to run any tool — the agent will get errors on every operation.

Complete the Configuration Wizard before using the MCP, or type /flx-setup in Claude Code: it guides you through creating or choosing the databases and writing ConfConnectionString and DataConnectionString. With them configured, the server works correctly.

docs.title: Troubleshooting: manual installation
docs.text:
If the MCP server doesn't start or the flexygo-mcp command isn't recognized, the automatic installation may not have completed correctly. First check whether the tool is installed:

Bash
dotnet tool list -g

Look for flexygo-mcp in the list. If it doesn't appear, install it manually:

Bash
dotnet tool install -g flexygo-mcp

If it's already installed but you want to update to the latest version:

Bash
dotnet tool update -g flexygo-mcp

docs.title: Basic use of the MCP server
Basic use of the MCP server
docs.text: Once the prerequisites are met, the project already includes everything needed to work with the MCP server from Claude Code.

docs.title: Opening the project in Claude Code
docs.text:
The project generated from the Flexygo template carries, at its root, the .mcp.json file, which tells Claude Code how to start the server, and .claude/settings.json, which turns it on for the project. There is nothing to start by hand: Claude Code launches the server when you open the project folder.

  1. Open the project folder in Claude Code: in the desktop app, in the VS Code extension, or in a terminal with claude from that folder.
  2. If Claude Code asks whether to use the project's flexygo server, accept.
  3. Type /mcp to check that the flexygo server shows as connected.

The first time it starts, the server installs the /flx-* commands and the Flexygo panel in the project. If the commands do not show when you type /flx-, open a new chat.

Before you start: spec-driven tools

If you use tools such as GSD, Spec Kit or others based on spec-driven development, do not combine them with the Flexygo MCP server. The context they generate interferes with the real context the MCP provides and degrades the agent's quality. See Best practices for more detail.

docs.title: First steps
docs.text:
The work is done with commands that start with /flx-, one phase at a time. To begin:

Situation Command A freshly created project, with no databases or connections /flx-setup prepares the databases and the connection strings. The first time you work on the project /flx-context gathers what the application is about and who uses it. You want a whole application /flx-build-product, with a description of what you want to build. You want to add something to a project that already has things built /flx-new-development, then /flx-plan. It is a small change to something that already exists /flx-fast. You do not know where you left off /flx-status.

For example:

Text Only
/flx-build-product I want a back office to manage a call center

The more specific your description, the better the agent's start. From there on, the agent tells you at every moment which command comes next.

See the whole flow, phase by phase, in Workflow with commands. The state of the work can also be seen in the panel and board, and what the agent builds with Flexygo 10, in What it builds on Flexygo 10.

Tips for better results

See Best practices for recommendations on how to ask for things and when to open a new chat.

docs.title: MCP server configuration
docs.text: The project generated from the Flexygo template already carries the configuration it needs. There is nothing to change to get started.

docs.title: The .mcp.json file
docs.text:
At the project root, .mcp.json tells Claude Code how to start the server:

JSON
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "flexygo": {
      "command": "flexygo-mcp",
      "env": {
        "ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT": "Development"
      }
    }
  }
}
  • command is the global flexygo-mcp tool, installed with the .NET 10 SDK (see Prerequisites).
  • ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT decides which of the Backend's appsettings files are read. With Development, appsettings.Development.json is read.

The project's .claude/settings.json file turns the flexygo server on, so Claude Code does not have to ask every time.

Design with Google Stitch

The template also carries a stitch entry in .mcp.json, which /flx-design uses to draw the screens. It needs the STITCH_API_KEY environment variable. If you do not use it, it does no harm.

docs.title: The databases
docs.text: The server has no connections of its own: it reads ConfConnectionString and DataConnectionString from the appsettings of the project's Backend. If they are not configured, /flx-setup guides you through creating or choosing the databases and writing them.

docs.title: Error telemetry
docs.text: Errors of the server's tools are recorded in a collector on the same computer. The FLEXYGO_MCP_ERROR_TELEMETRY environment variable sends them to another collector, or turns them off with off. See Error telemetry.

docs.title: Security checks
docs.text:
The server reads some addresses from files that travel with the project, such as launchSettings.json or appsettings.json. A cloned project could bring them changed, so the server checks them before using them:

  • Application addresses. The panel, the board and the tools/app.ps1 script only use an http or https address on this computer (localhost, 127.0.0.1 or [::1]). Only its scheme, computer and port are taken. Anything else is ignored, and nothing is opened or started with it: a scheme such as file:, an address on another computer, or text added after the address.
  • Cache reload. To reload the application's cache, the server signs in with your user and password. If the Backend is on this computer, it does so without asking. If it is on another computer, it sends nothing: the agent tells you that computer's exact name and asks whether you want to send your credentials to it. Only with your yes, and only to that computer, does it sign in. With the Backend on this computer, it can use the test user's password kept in *.InterfaceTest/appsettings.local.json, as long as git ignores that file; it never repeats it or writes it anywhere, and if it is missing or wrong, it asks you for it.
  • Protected files. The agent cannot read or print the file with the test users' passwords (*.InterfaceTest/appsettings.local.json): it is told what to use instead. Nor can it write from the console inside .flexygo/, which only the server's tools write.
  • Secrets in git. The project's status warns if a conf/appsettings*.json tracked by git holds secrets, never showing their value.

docs.title: MCP tools and resources
docs.text: The flexygo-mcp server exposes tools the agent uses to work on the Flexygo project: reading and creating objects, properties, pages, modules, processes, security, tests… You don't need to know them: the /flx-* commands and the agent itself use them according to what you ask for.

docs.title: Exploring the available tools
docs.text:
In Claude Code, type /mcp and choose the flexygo server to see whether it is connected and the list of its tools.

While the agent works, the chat shows each tool it calls. That way you see what it is reading or changing in the project.

docs.title: MCP Apps
docs.text: Besides the data tools, the server includes three MCP Apps: interactive visual interfaces that the agent can open in response to specific requests. They show in clients that display MCP Apps.

docs.title: Flexygo Schema Diagram UI
docs.text:
An interactive diagram of the project's database model, with hierarchy and relationships between entities. Useful for visualizing the current schema before making changes or for understanding the structure of an existing project.

How to use it:

Text Only
Show me the project's current database model

The diagram shows the project's tables, columns, types, and foreign keys

docs.title: Color Picker UI
docs.text:
An interactive color picker. Once a color is confirmed, the agent automatically modifies the application's two main variables: the header color and the navigation color.

How to use it:

Text Only
Change the application's main color to a dark corporate blue using the color picker

Pick the color and press "Apply color to project" for the agent to apply the change

docs.title: Flexygo Page Designer UI
docs.text:
A preview of the page designer: shows the available positions (slots) on each page and the modules configured in each one. Useful for reviewing the layout before making modifications.

How to use it:

Text Only
Open the page designer to see which modules are on each page

The designer shows the selected page's layout with its positions and assigned modules

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text: These recommendations assume the flexygo-mcp server is connected to Claude Code. If you haven't set it up yet, see Basic use first.

docs.title: Recommended model
docs.text: Use a current Claude model. For thinking and deciding (/flx-context, /flx-plan, /flx-discuss), use the most capable model you have; for executing a block already decided (/flx-execute, /flx-verify), a faster and cheaper one is enough.

docs.title: Managing the context window
docs.text:
This is the factor that most affects the quality of the work with the agent. As the conversation grows, the agent starts to lose coherence, forgets earlier instructions and makes mistakes it wouldn't make with a clean context. Every message in a long conversation also costs more.

Practical rules:

  • A new chat for each phase or block. The server keeps a checkpoint of each development, so a new chat resumes the work without rereading the previous conversation: type /flx-status or the next command. See Resuming the work.
  • Heed the status line's warning. When the context fills up, the Flexygo status line says so with context N% → new chat.
  • Don't use the same conversation to plan and to execute. The analysis or discussion phase uses up context that is then needed for the execution.
  • For /flx-build-product, always start with a clean context.

docs.title: Spec-driven development tools (GSD, Spec Kit, and similar)
docs.text:
Don't use spec-driven tools alongside the MCP server

Tools like GSD, Spec Kit, or others based on spec-driven development gather large amounts of project context (file structure, history, decisions, plans, etc.). However, they should not be used together with the Flexygo MCP server.

Why?

The MCP server already injects its own specialized context about the state of the application and the database. These planning tools don't have real access to how the application works or to the DB structure, so the context they generate doesn't reflect the reality of the Flexygo project.

The result is counterproductive: the context they gather interferes with the real context the MCP provides and occupies context window space with information that has no operational value. The agent ends up working with contradictory signals.

Use the MCP server directly, without additional layers of spec-driven planning. For complex tasks, follow the advice in the Managing the context window section and break the work into steps.

docs.title: Follow the command flow
docs.text: The /flx-* commands take the work phase by phase: context, plan, decisions, execution block by block, review, verification, tests, quality, help and, if needed, the API. Each phase is the gate to the next, so you don't need to remember what comes next: the agent, the panel and /flx-status tell you. See the whole flow.

docs.title: Always identify the object you're working on
docs.text:
When you want to modify something, explicitly state what it is and what it's called. The agent works with a project that can have dozens of modules, entities, or pages — without that context, it interprets or asks.

Too vagueEffective Text Only
Modify the listing module so it also shows the phone number
Text Only
In the "CustomerList" module (Customer entity), add the Phone property
as a visible column in the grid. The field already exists on the entity.

docs.title: Set boundaries for the task's scope
docs.text:
State what shouldn't be touched. Agents tend to be more creative than necessary when the scope isn't clear.

Text Only
I want to change the header color to #1a3a5c.
Use the Color Picker MCP App. Don't modify anything else about the style.

docs.title: Split the phases when the task is complex
docs.text:
If a task has several parts, ask for them in steps and wait for confirmation between them. Don't throw everything into a single prompt.

A prompt that can spiral out of controlSame work, under control Text Only
Create the Order entity, add the relationship with Customer, generate the
creation form, and update the navigation menu

Text Only
Step 1: Create the Order entity with the fields: id, date, total, customerId (FK to Customer).
Once you have it, confirm and wait.
(After confirmation) Text Only
Step 2: Generate the creation form for the Order entity.
Once you have it, confirm and wait.

docs.title: Ask for a review before running data changes
docs.text:
For any operation that modifies the database, ask the agent to describe what it's going to do before executing it:

Text Only
Before running any change to the database, explain exactly which
operations you're going to perform and wait for my confirmation.

docs.title: Give context at the start of each conversation
docs.text:
If the task starts from a specific state of the project, orient the agent before asking for anything:

Text Only
I'm in the "OrderManagement" module. The Order entity has the fields:
id, date, total, status (enum: Pending/Shipped/Delivered), customerId.
I want to add a status filter in the main listing.

The agent will work on what you describe to it — don't assume it "knows" the current state of your project.

docs.title: Tips for using Claude Code
docs.text:
• If the agent doesn't use the Flexygo tools when it should, remind it explicitly: "Use the Flexygo MCP tools for this".
  • When the agent proposes several approaches, pick one before continuing. Sustained ambiguity uses up context without progress.
  • If an answer was wrong, correct it in the next message before continuing with the task — don't ignore it or the agent will build on the error.
  • When you update the server (dotnet tool update -g flexygo-mcp), open a new chat: a chat already under way keeps the tools it started with.

docs.title: Verify that the agent is using the tools
docs.text:
The Claude Code chat shows in real time which tools the agent is calling. If the agent doesn't show any Flexygo tool being used, it's making the answer up — it isn't reading or changing anything real in the project.

Signs that the agent is hallucinating instead of using the MCP:

  • It answers immediately without showing any tool call
  • It describes entities or structures that don't match your real project
  • The changes it "made" don't show up in the application

If it happens, stop the conversation, check with /mcp that the flexygo server is connected, and explicitly ask the agent to use the Flexygo tools.

docs.title: Make a checkpoint commit before iterating
docs.text:
When you close a block or a development and have reviewed and approved it, make a Git commit before continuing with requests for improvements or individual changes.

This checkpoint has several advantages:

  • You have a clear point to return to if a later iteration breaks something
  • The agent can see exactly what changed in each task (clean diff)
  • You keep control of what is "approved base" and what are later changes

It's good practice to commit often as you go — don't wait until the product is finished.

docs.title: Adjust the complexity of what you ask for
docs.text:
A small change to something that already exists goes through /flx-fast, with no plan. Anything that creates tables or entities, touches permissions or loads data goes through /flx-new-development and /flx-plan, which splits it into blocks.

In any case, it's the user's responsibility not to ask for tasks that are too complex or have too many open fronts at once. The more variables a request has, the more likely the result won't be what was expected or the agent will lose coherence halfway through.

If the task you have in mind seems big, split it yourself before giving it to the agent.

docs.title: Workflow with commands
docs.text:
New in version 10.0

You can now create a Flexygo application by talking to an assistant connected to the MCP. The assistant gathers the requirements, asks you questions before starting, proposes a design and organises the work into blocks and tasks. It then builds the application and opens it in the browser so you can check it.

You can also open a board from the assistant to follow tasks, decisions, history and quality checks.

With Claude Code, the Flexygo MCP server is driven by commands that start with /flx-. Each command is a phase, and each phase is the gate to the next one: the agent does not skip a phase or guess which one it is in. It talks to you in your words: it explains what it does at each step, without tool names. If one of its messages names one, it is handed back to be written again.

Can't see the commands?

The commands are installed in the project the first time the server starts. If they do not show when you type /flx-, ask the agent to sync the Flexygo commands and open a new chat.

docs.title: The flow, in order
docs.text:
Command What it is for /flx-context First reads the material you left in the project's Resources/ folder. Then gathers the context: the business, the prefixes, the conventions and who uses the application (roles, public screens, and whether anyone will use it from outside). Writes ONBOARDING.md at the project root and a short description of the application, the first thing the board shows. /flx-plan Turns the request into blocks with their task list. If the application has several roles, the plan carries a security task; if it has screens, it ends with demo data. Each block fits in one chat (see Blocks sized to a chat). If the development has an offline app, it rejects auto-numbered keys (IDENTITY) and says why: GUID keys are needed. /flx-discuss Closes the plan's open points one at a time and records each decision. On Flexygo 10 it also asks what the Ctrl+K search should find. /flx-execute Builds one block, task by task, and when it finishes verifies it by itself with the recorded walks. It tells you in one line how it went and which block comes next. When it starts, it gets what you already decided for its tasks and does not ask you again. /flx-review Compares what was agreed with what was built, and brings the application's description up to date if what was built changes it. /flx-verify Checks in the browser that it works, by replaying the recorded walks. /flx-execute already does it when it closes each block; by hand it checks everything again. /flx-test Writes the product's own tests and leaves them green. /flx-quality Looks for what is missing (pager, empty state, way back…) and records your decision on each finding. It sweeps the whole catalogue as well as what you point out, and only calls a fix good once it is seen on screen with the role that uses it and with the contrast measured. /flx-help Gives the application its help for the end user: a help centre with a guide per flow and role, a welcome tour per role, a guided tour per screen and field help. See The application's help. /flx-api Only if the application is used from outside: exposes what was built through the WebAPI, read-only by default and per role, and tests it with one user of each role.

At any time, as well:

  • /flx-status says where the work stands and what comes next.
  • /flx-origin says which origin new work lands in.
  • /flx-build-product walks the whole flow for "an application for…".
  • /flx-new-development starts new work in a project that already has things built.

docs.title: Small changes: /flx-fast
docs.text:
A minor change to something that already exists (a property, a label, a filter, a module, a list) needs no plan and no blocks: /flx-fast makes it and keeps a record.

If the change is bigger, /flx-fast sends it to /flx-new-development. It is bigger if it does any of these:

  • creates new tables or entities;
  • touches permissions;
  • loads data;
  • deletes an entity;
  • adds up to more than about five changes.

It only asks before starting if the change deletes something or is ambiguous.

docs.title: The model for each phase
docs.text:
Each phase is best done with a model, and the agent recommends the one for the phase the project is in, in bold and with its reason:

Phases Recommended model Why /flx-plan, /flx-discuss, /flx-review and /flx-quality Opus They are phases of thinking and deciding. The rest Sonnet They are phases of building and checking.

You decide: switch model (/model opus, for example), keep yours, or always keep yours. If you keep yours, it does not ask again in that phase; if you say always, it does not ask again in this project. The agent never switches model on its own.

If you would rather it switched by itself, turn on the environment variable FLEXYGO_MODEL_PER_PHASE=auto; it is off by default. With it, each command carries its model, and /flx-status and /flx-origin, which only read where the work stands, use Haiku. Claude Code uses it for the turn in which you type the command, and with your next message it goes back to the session's model.

docs.title: Blocks sized to a chat
docs.text:
/flx-plan sizes each block to fit in one chat: what one /flx-execute builds, checks on screen and records before the chat fills up, about 150 turns. What counts is not the number of tasks but the screens with rules of their own: a block carries two or three at most, and a bigger one is split by screen. On the other hand, the data model or many offline screens copied from a template fit in a single block.

If tasks have to be added to a block later, they go at its end with their origin: nothing is renumbered, so assumptions and dependencies keep pointing at their task.

docs.title: Version control
docs.text:
When preparing the project. If the product's folder is not in git, /flx-setup and /flx-build-product offer to put it there, step by step and only with your yes:

  1. install git, if it is not found;
  2. start the repository with the template's .gitignore;
  3. set a local identity for this project's commits;
  4. make a first commit, without files that hold secrets.

If you say no, it is recorded and you are not asked again.

When each block closes. If the product is in git and the block closed well, the agent offers a local commit of the block, with the message "B-n: block title". It offers it at the start of the next chat, before its first task, together with the other end-of-block questions; the last block offers it when it closes.

  • It shows you the files first, and leaves out the configuration files that hold secrets.
  • If the block's configuration is not in files yet, it says so and offers to put it there before the commit.
  • It never pushes.
  • A "no" counts for that block; if you say no for the whole project, it does not ask again.

The project's status also warns if a conf/appsettings*.json tracked by git holds secrets: it names the file and the kind of key, never the value, and says how to stop tracking it.

docs.title: The project's material: the Resources/ folder
docs.text:
Leave in the project's Resources/ folder the material it is built from: requirements, sample data, screenshots, logos or links. You can copy it by hand or upload it from the board. The folder travels with git.

/flx-context reads everything it can read in that folder before asking you anything, sums up what it brings and marks it as reviewed. If you add files later, run /flx-context again: it reads only the new ones.

docs.title: The application's help: /flx-help
docs.text:
/flx-help writes the help the end user will see inside the application itself. Before writing anything it proposes what it will do and waits for your yes.

  • The help centre. An index page, ordered by role, with a search box and a guide per workflow. Each guide tells the work from start to end, screen by screen, with its screenshots on the demo data. It opens from the Help menu option and from a button on each screen's bar.
  • The welcome tour. One per role, on its start page. It is offered by itself the first time the user enters and does not come back. On each page, each role sees a single invitation.
  • A guided tour per screen and field help.
  • The offline app's guides. If the development has an offline app, each role that uses it gets a guide of its work on the phone and another one on synchronising: when to sync, what goes up and what comes down, and how to tell a change has arrived. They are in the same help centre, under their role, and open from the phone's or the computer's browser.

The help's texts are in the product's language. If a product's help was written with an earlier version of the server, run /flx-help again to redo it in the new format.

The help centre: search box, welcome tour and one guide per flow, grouped by role

docs.title: Cheaper verification: recorded walks
docs.text:
/flx-verify no longer has the agent look at every screen again, and /flx-execute applies it to the block it has just built. Each screen has a walk: a browser route recorded in a file of the interface test project. Each development keeps its own in its own folder, {Product}.InterfaceTest/walks/<development>/; the ones that already existed without a folder count for the active development. It is product code: it travels with git and also runs in continuous integration.

When verifying, the server replays every walk at once, in a single browser:

  • A walk that passes against its accepted baseline is recorded as "seen working", with its capture. You are not asked to look at that screen again.
  • A walk that fails is recorded red and reopens its task, the one of its own development, even if another development has a task with the same number.
  • A new or changed capture comes back to you with the difference painted in red. You open it, look at it, and accept or reject it. What you accept is recorded.

Each capture is also measured on its own: contrast, untranslated identifiers, broken images, sideways scroll and the order of lists.

The saving is that the agent only deals with what fails or changes, instead of going through every screen one by one.

The captures the agent takes with the browser go to the project's .playwright-mcp/ folder. If one is left loose at the root, the project's status says so.

docs.title: Permissions to verify
docs.text:
Before a block's first task, the agent asks you at once for the permissions it needs to verify. Once the development has your answer, it does not ask again; if you say no, it asks you in every block:

  • create and delete test data (TEST);
  • start and stop the application;
  • lock and unlock the test users while each role is tested.

The walks run without opening windows, in user turns: each role signs in alone, with the other test users locked, and at the end everything is left as it was. They are replayed in the light theme of their captures, and each user gets their theme back at the end. Real users are never touched. Without the permission to lock, the agent says so and does not try.

Evaluation licence

An evaluation licence only admits, at once, the administrator and one more user; that is why the other test users are locked before signing in with each role. If the licence rejects a sign-in, the agent says so ("Invalid license…") and not as a credentials failure, and a locked user is named as locked, not as a timeout.

docs.title: The product's own tests
docs.text:
/flx-test writes tests that stay in the product's repository, in its two test projects:

  • {Product}.UnitTest: at least one test for each new process or business rule.
  • {Product}.InterfaceTest: at least one walk for each new screen. It checks that the screen opens without errors, that its main action works and that the effect shows.

The agent proposes the list to you in business terms and waits for your yes. Each test creates its own data and deletes it at the end, without touching the demo data.

Before calling the tests good, the agent breaks one on purpose, sees it fail and puts it back to green. The unit tests run in continuous integration before every publication. The interface tests need the application to be running. They are recorded like the walks: in user turns, without windows and in the light theme. A rejected sign-in closes its browser and is not retried.

If you decide to go without tests, that is recorded as a decision.

docs.title: Resuming without paying for the whole conversation
docs.text:
Resuming a long conversation is expensive: the model reads all of it again. So for each development the server keeps a checkpoint of about 2 KB with the essentials:

  • the phase and the block;
  • the open decisions;
  • the last verification result;
  • the known incidents;
  • what comes next.

To carry on another day, or when the chat is getting heavy:

  1. Open a new chat.
  2. Type /flx-status, or just the next command of the flow.

The agent starts from the checkpoint, not from the previous conversation. The panel's band shows how full the chat is and, from 70 %, offers New chat and go on, which does both steps at once. See How full the chat is. In a terminal there is no band: the status line under the text box warns with context N% → new chat from 80 %.

docs.title: Lessons carry over from one chat to the next
docs.text:
Each block starts with the project's lessons: the platform limits already found and the corrections you made to the agent. They come from the project, not from the conversation or a handover message, so a new chat does not trip over the same thing again. When you ask the agent to remember something, it records it, and the next block already knows.

When a block closes, the agent also records what is left open: a limit, a question or a pending decision. The next block gets it even if nobody tells it when the chat opens.

docs.title: Error telemetry
docs.text:
When one of the server's tools fails, the server records what is needed to reproduce the failure:

  • the tool and its arguments, with passwords and SQL values masked;
  • the error;
  • the versions;
  • the phase and task where it happened.

It never sends the conversation or the rows of a query.

By default, errors go to an OpenTelemetry collector on the same computer (http://localhost:7472), so they do not leave it. The server's first answer in each session reminds you of this.

To send them to another collector, put its address in the FLEXYGO_MCP_ERROR_TELEMETRY environment variable. To turn it off:

Bash
FLEXYGO_MCP_ERROR_TELEMETRY=off

docs.title: Panel and board
docs.text: The state of the flow can also be seen without asking: in the Flexygo panel, above the chat, and on the developer's board. See Panel and board.

docs.title: What it builds on Flexygo 10
docs.text: With a project on Flexygo 10, the agent uses what this version brings: ECharts charts, KPI cards, rules on save, live notices, REST objects, brand and account screens. See What it builds on Flexygo 10.

docs.title: Panel and board
docs.text:
While you work with the agent, the Flexygo MCP server shows where the development stands without you having to ask. It does so in two places:

  • The Flexygo panel, inside Claude Code, beside the chat.
  • The developer's board, a page in the browser with all the detail.

docs.title: The band above the chat
docs.text:
In the Claude Code desktop app and in the VS Code extension, the panel is a band above the text box with three parts: Now (the phase and the command that comes next), Your call (what is waiting for a decision of yours) and Next.

"Next" and what is left to close come from the same list, in your words; if there is more than one thing, the rest unfolds below.

The band has three modes: full, lite and off.

  • Full also shows cards with the task ring, what is left to close, how the last block's verification went and how full the chat is.
  • Off leaves a single pill, Flexygo ▸, to open it again. Typing /flexygo also brings it back.

Its buttons:

Button What it does Go Writes the command that comes next in the text box, without sending it. Start apps / Stop apps Starts or stops the product's Backend and Frontend, with a dot that says whether they answer. It uses the product's tools/app.ps1 script, which the server adds if it is missing. Board Opens the board on the tab that matters now: Decisions if a decision is open, Resources if there are files not yet reviewed and, otherwise, the last one you looked at. Live view Shows the screen being built (see below).

If the buttons do not fit in one row, Live view and the apps buttons move to a … menu. Each open decision carries one button per option, with the recommended one marked.

There is no verify button: when a block closes, /flx-execute verifies it by itself and the band only shows how it went. The band is in Spanish.

The panel also records the time and API usage price of each /flx-* command, subagents included. They are kept per project on this computer. The band shows no money: the price is on the board.

docs.title: How full the chat is
docs.text:
The band shows how much context the chat has used: context N %. The fuller it is, the worse the agent answers, so it warns in time:

  • Below 70 %, there is room left in this chat.
  • From 70 %, it asks you to finish the current step and carry on in a new chat.
  • From 80 %, it warns that from there on it answers worse.

The warnings quote the real percentage, for example "Context at 82 %: …".

From 70 % the New chat and go on button shows. It clears the chat (/clear) and, in the new chat, runs the command that comes next. Nothing is lost: the agent carries on from the development's checkpoint, not from the conversation.

If Claude Code does not let the panel clear the chat, the band asks you to send /clear yourself. The next command is already kept, and runs by itself when the new chat starts if you do it within 10 minutes.

In the terminal

With Claude Code in a terminal there is no band: the panel opens as a side pane with the same information. That pane also has the Project button, which opens ONBOARDING.md, and ES / EN to change the language.

docs.title: Live view
docs.text:
Live view opens the board on the Live tab: the application beside a chat with Claude. See Live: the application and the chat with Claude.

The button shows when the product has its Frontend; if the Frontend does not answer, the board starts it.

docs.title: The developer's board
docs.text:
The board brings together on one page what is done and what is pending, what is left to verify, the API usage price and time per command, the data model, the decisions and the quality findings. It shows every Flexygo project on this computer, with its developments, except test benches: copies of another project and folders marked with a .flexygo-bench file. The project you open always shows.

The Overview: what the application is, its context and the next step

Its tabs are Overview, Live, Kanban, Dependencies, History, Decisions, Model, Screens, Quality and Resources. The Copy next command button puts the command that comes next on the clipboard, and ES / EN changes the language.

The Overview opens with what the application is, in two or three sentences: what it is for, for whom and its main flow. /flx-context writes it and /flx-review keeps it current. Below, in short lines, the business, the users and roles, the flow, your decisions, whether it is used from outside and what has been built.

docs.title: How to open it
docs.text:
• From the band, with the Board button.
  • By hand, from the project folder:
Bash
flexygo-mcp --board

With --tab decisions it opens straight on that tab.

The board opens only when you ask for it. It is served by a small local server that only answers on this computer and stops by itself after 30 minutes without use; each chat message counts as use. If the project has no Frontend, the board is a static page.

docs.title: API usage price
docs.text:
The board shows the API usage price: what the agent's work would cost at Anthropic API prices. It is worked out the way Claude Code works out /cost, with its price table per model and the real tokens of each turn.

  • In History, per command and per phase.
  • In Kanban and Dependencies, the development's total.

If you use Claude Code with a subscription, that is not what you pay: the real cost is not known. It is there to compare phases and developments with each other. It only shows on the board: the band shows no money.

docs.title: Resources
docs.text:
The Resources tab shows the project's Resources/ folder: the material it is built from. Drop files there, or choose them, to upload them; you can also add a link with a note on what it is and why it matters.

  • It takes images, PDF, Office documents, CSV, text, JSON, XML and zip, up to 50 MB per file and 300 MB in all.
  • Each file shows as new until /flx-context reads it, and then as reviewed.
  • To upload files, the board has to be opened from the project and served with its Frontend.

docs.title: Live: the application and the chat with Claude
docs.text:
The Live tab shows the application beside a conversation with Claude. The board itself serves the chat by calling Claude Code on this computer, so it keeps working even if you close the editor.

  • At the top you choose the project's conversation, or start one with + New. The answer arrives as it is generated, and ■ Stop cuts it.
  • If another window has just written in that same conversation, the board shows it as open in that window and does not let you write in it, so two do not write at once. Write there or open a new one here.
  • From the board, Claude may only use Flexygo's tools. If it tries another one, a Permission refused card shows what it wanted to do; Allow this time and retry lets it through that once.
  • It needs Claude Code installed and signed in on this computer. If either is missing, the board says so in a card.

Cost

Each message of the board's chat loads the project's context again, so it costs more than a message in the editor's chat.

The application on the Live tab, with Select, Pause and Full screen

With Select you ask for changes on the application itself:

  1. Press Select.
  2. Click what you want to change: a page, a module, a field, a column, a button, a menu option…
  3. Answer What should change? and press Send (or Enter). Esc cancels.

The message reaches the conversation saying which element it is about.

docs.title: How to turn on the panel and the board
One-time step: --enable-panel
docs.text:
The panel is a Claude Code add-on that ships inside the Flexygo MCP server. For Claude Code to know about it, run this once per user and computer, in a terminal:

Bash
flexygo-mcp --enable-panel

This command does two things, and nothing else:

  1. It copies the panel to the ~/.flexygo-mcp/mods folder, which is kept when you update the server.
  2. It adds one entry to your Claude Code user settings (~/.claude/settings.json) that tells it where the panel is.

You do not need to remember the command: when this step is missing, /flx-setup asks whether you want to turn it on and only runs it with your yes. The server never runs it on its own, because it writes to your user settings.

Each project turns the panel on in its own .claude/settings.json, and the server does that by itself when it starts. If someone turned it off in a project, it stays off.

The panel shows when you open a new chat or session of Claude Code in the project.

docs.title: Where it works
docs.text:
Where you use Claude Code What you see Desktop app The band above the chat. Live view opens the board on the Live tab. VS Code extension The band above the chat, with the mode in a drop-down. Live view opens the board on the Live tab. Terminal A side pane instead of the band. No interface (claude -p) Nothing to see, but each command's API usage price is still recorded.

The board does not depend on the panel: it is a browser page and works in every case, also with flexygo-mcp --board.

Coming soon

In an upcoming version the panel will install with one click, with no commands.

docs.title: What it builds on Flexygo 10
docs.text: With a project on Flexygo 10, the MCP server uses what this version brings: ECharts charts, KPI cards, rules on save, live notices, REST objects, brand and account screens…

docs.title: ECharts charts and themes
docs.text:
On Flexygo 10 every chart is ECharts: ten types (bars, lines, doughnut, radar…). It can also:

  • put the total in the centre of a doughnut;
  • add a target line;
  • put the unit after every figure;
  • add a footer line with the change ("+12% vs last month").

Figures follow the user's language format (35,000 in English, 35.000 in Spanish).

If you ask for no theme, the chart uses Flexygo 10's default one. It can also create a theme of the product's own, with its colours and the shapes of one of the factory themes, without touching the factory themes, which every application shares.

The same chart with the factory themes and, on the right, a theme of its own created by the agent

docs.title: KPI cards
docs.text:
KPI modules (easy info) are drawn as cards. A card can carry:

  • the change and the trend;
  • a target with its progress bar;
  • a small chart of the evolution;
  • action links;
  • a period switch (24 h, 7 days, 30 days), which remembers the user's choice.

The colour follows the skin and dark mode.

A card with a target, the change and the evolution

docs.title: Rules on save and decisions
docs.text:
For what must happen when a record is saved, the agent creates an object rule instead of a scheduled job. The rule fires on insert, update or delete, and can carry conditions:

  • the record matches a condition;
  • a column has changed;
  • a column has changed to a given value.

What it does can be:

  • send a notice to the bell of a role or a user;
  • send an email;
  • create or update records;
  • run a process;
  • ask for a decision: a task with options, a deadline and escalation, approved or rejected from the bell or from the record.
A rule asks to approve notes over €1,000: the decision shows on the record and in the bell

docs.title: Live notices
docs.text:
The agent can turn on an object's live notices, so connected users see the records others save without reloading. Object security, per-user filters and hidden properties are respected.

What reaches each module, in the 2026 skin:

Module Inserts Updates and deletes List Yes: a "Show them" strip on the module bar No Planner Yes No Kanban Yes: it draws the card No Calendar Yes Yes Timeline No No Another page Yes: a notice at the bottom right No

Live notices are not added to the bell. To notify in the bell, use a rule on save.

Another user has added a work order: the list says so and shows it on "Show them"

docs.title: REST objects
docs.text: An object can keep its records in another system, behind a REST API. The agent registers the service, with its address, authentication and paging, and then creates the objects that read from it. The service's key is never repeated in the answers.

docs.title: Brand, account screens and maintenance
docs.text:
The agent places the brand files with the names Flexygo 10 expects:

  • the logo and its variant for dark backgrounds;
  • the symbol for the folded sidebar;
  • the browser icon;
  • the image of the account screens and the one of the maintenance page.

It also styles the sign-in and the maintenance page. It never turns maintenance mode on or off: an administrator does that.

The product's logo in the sidebar, light and dark

docs.title: What the platform already does well stays
docs.text:
A design reference (a mock-up, a screenshot, a screen from another tool) may lack something Flexygo 10 already does well: the top bar with the notices bell and the Ctrl+K search, the control panel or the user menu. The reference leaving it out is no reason to remove it: it is the reference that is wrong.

  • The agent never removes or hides a working platform element on its own. It only does so if you decide it, and the decision is recorded.
  • When comparing with the reference, that difference closes as "the reference is wrong": the platform's element stays, with a note saying which one.
  • Putting the brand in the side panel does not remove the top bar.
  • After every block, the quality review checks that the top bar is still there with its bell, that Ctrl+K opens the search and finds a record, and that every menu option has its label. Verification looks at every screen in light and in dark, in the user's language.
The Stitch reference and the built screen: it follows its design and keeps the top bar with the Ctrl+K search and the bell

docs.title: More of Flexygo 10
docs.text:
• Process security with a condition: a process allowed or denied to a role only when a condition holds.
  • Tabs in forms: a long form is split into tabs.
  • Toolbar buttons: the agent marks each module's main button and decides which ones fold into the … menu.
  • Calendar: working hours, overlaps, the "now" line and the rest of the Flexygo 10 calendar options.
  • New settings, such as hiding the news or allowing users to sign up.

docs.title: Search with Ctrl+K
docs.text:
In /flx-discuss, once the data model is settled, the agent asks one question: which collections the Ctrl+K search should find, and by which fields. It proposes three to five collections with two or three fields each, and you add, drop or say none. Each user only sees the groups of the objects they may see. The names of the groups and objects show in English even when the user works in another language: it is a platform limit.

The search finds a customer by name; the group and the object show in English

docs.title: Screen texts in English, translated
docs.text: Labels, buttons, tabs, titles, menu options and guided tour steps are written in English, the original the platform translates from. In the same step, the agent translates them into the project's language and every other active language. That way a user who works in English never sees texts in Spanish.

docs.title: CI/CD — Overview
docs.text: This section summarizes a generic CI/CD flow applicable to GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, TeamCity, and Azure Pipelines. The idea is that each platform executes the same steps using its specific syntax.

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text:
• CI (Continuous Integration): build, test, analyze, and generate artifacts on every change.
  • CD (Continuous Deployment): version, publish, and deploy in a repeatable and traceable way.

docs.title: Minimum pipeline steps
docs.text:
1. Trigger: on push, pull_request, or merge.
  2. Checkout the repo.
  3. Prepare the environment:
    • In our case, .NET 9 SDK.
  4. Restore dependencies:
    • dotnet restore
  5. Build the Solution:
    • dotnet build ProjectName.sln -c Release
  6. Publish Frontend:
    • dotnet publish ProjectName.Frontend.csproj -c Release --no-build
  7. Publish Backend:
    • dotnet publish ProjectName.Backend.csproj -c Release --no-build
  8. Build Configuration DB:
    • dotnet build ProjectName.Conf.Database.sqlproj -c Release --no-build
  9. Build Data DB (optional):
    • dotnet build ProjectName.Data.Database.sqlproj -c Release --no-build
  10. Unit tests:
    • dotnet test ProjectName.UnitTest.csproj -c Release --no-build
  11. Interface tests:
    • dotnet test ProjectName.InterfaceTest.csproj -c Release --no-build
  12. NuGet generation:
    • With Nuspec (Default):
      • nuget pack ProjectName.Frontend.nuspec -Properties Configuration=Release
      • nuget pack ProjectName.Backend.nuspec -Properties Configuration=Release
      • nuget pack ProjectName.Conf.Database.nuspec -Properties Configuration=Release
      • nuget pack ProjectName.Data.Database.nuspec -Properties Configuration=Release
    • With dotnet:
      • dotnet pack ProjectName.Frontend.csproj -c Release --no-build
      • dotnet pack ProjectName.Backend.csproj -c Release --no-build
      • dotnet pack ProjectName.Conf.Database.sqlproj -c Release --no-build
      • dotnet pack ProjectName.Data.Database.sqlproj -c Release --no-build
  13. Docker image generation:
    • docker build -t Repository/Name:Version -f Dockerfile PublicacionProjectName
    • The database one, also with --build-arg DAC_VERSION=Version (why).

docs.title: TeamCity
docs.text:
Flexygo products are built in TeamCity from a common template, Template flexygo products core. Each product creates its build configuration from it and only fills in its parameters: the steps, the artifacts and the version number come from the template.

For the general idea of the pipeline, valid in any tool, see the overview.

docs.title: Creating a product's configuration
docs.text:
1. In TeamCity, inside the products project, create a new Build Configuration from the Template flexygo products core template.
  2. Fill in its parameters under Parameters:
Parameter What it is Example ProductName Prefix of the solution's projects, those of the product template: <ProductName>.Frontend, .Backend, .Conf.Database, .Data.Database, .UnitTest and .InterfaceTest MyProduct ProductGitUrl Address of the product's repository — ProductBranch Branch that is built develop DEVEXPRESS_API Key of the DevExpress NuGet feed — env.msbuild.debugrelease Build configuration release

Credentials

Keys and passwords (DevExpress's, the test databases' SQL Server one, the one to publish NuGets) go in parameters of type Password, so TeamCity masks them in the build logs. They are never written in a step's text.

The parameters inherited from the template, filled in for a product; the DevExpress key is masked

The configuration uses the products' common VCS root with clean checkout, so every build starts from a clean copy.

docs.title: The steps
docs.text:
The template has 19 steps. They group like this:

The template's 19 steps, with their type, what they run and when: the last one runs even if something failed before (step names in Spanish)

docs.title: 1. Restore
docs.text: Step What it does Restore NuGet packages dotnet restore <ProductName>.sln with four sources: nuget.org, DevExpress (with %DEVEXPRESS_API%) and Flexygo's two NuGet feeds, the stable and the beta one.

docs.title: 2. Publish
docs.text:
Step What it does Publish frontend dotnet publish in Release to publish\<ProductName>\<ProductName>.Frontend, with Version, FileVersion and InformationalVersion (the build number and the commit). Publish backend The same, to publish\<ProductName>\<ProductName>.Backend. Publish the product's unit tests Publishes the <ProductName>.UnitTest project into the published Backend's folder.

Node.js on the agent

The Frontend compiles TypeScript with node. If the agent does not have it, publishing the Frontend fails with MSB6003.

docs.title: 3. Databases
docs.text:
Step What it does Build the CONFIG database dotnet build of <ProductName>.Conf.Database.sqlproj in Release, with /p:DacVersion=%build.number%. Publish the CONFIG database Publishes the dacpac with sqlpackage /Action:Publish to a test database, <ProductName>BD_IC, on the test SQL Server: it creates it from scratch, with the dacpac version equal to the build number. If sqlpackage fails, the step fails. Build the data database The same with <ProductName>.Data.Database.sqlproj. Publish the data database The same, to the product's test database.

So every build checks that both databases really build and publish, not only that the project compiles.

docs.title: 4. Start the application and test
docs.text:
Step What it does Create the start file Writes publish\<ProductName>\run_windows.bat, which starts the Frontend and the Backend with Kestrel. Change the test config file Keeps a clean copy of the published conf\appsettings.json files and gives them the test databases' connection strings, the local addresses (Frontend http://localhost:7111, Backend http://localhost:7110/api/backend/) and mail as configured. Starts the application and checks that it answers. Run the unit tests dotnet test of Flexygo.UnitTest.dll, the core's tests, from the published Backend's folder. Run the product's unit tests dotnet test of <ProductName>.UnitTest.csproj. Run the interface tests dotnet test of <ProductName>.InterfaceTest.csproj, against the running application. Clean appsettings Deletes the published appsettings.local.json files and puts back the clean appsettings.json: it undoes the "Change the test config file" step.

The three test steps use the .NET 6 SDK.

docs.title: 5. Generate the NuGets
docs.text:
Step What it does Generate the Frontend NuGet NuGet pack of <ProductName>.Frontend.nuspec, with the version equal to the build number, to publish/, and publishes the package. Generate the Backend and Library NuGets The same with <ProductName>.Backend.nuspec and <ProductName>.Library.nuspec. Generate the CONFIG database NuGet The same with <ProductName>.Conf.Database.nuspec. Generate the data database NuGet The same with <ProductName>.Data.Database.nuspec.

All five use NuGet.CommandLine 6.12.2.

docs.title: 6. Stop
docs.text:
